entries.name: Detox / cleanse products
entries.why: Mostly laxatives or water pills; they name no actual toxin.
entries.source: 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
entries.verdict_text: Tier 1, dosed to your blood level
entries.why: Clearly fixes a true shortage. If you are not low, a bigger dose does not buy you extra health (VITAL and D-Health found no drop in cancer, heart events or fractures in people who were not low). It lowered colds a little, mostly in people who started low.
entries.dose_text: Maintenance 1,000-4,000 IU a day; correct a low level 2,000-5,000 IU a day; very low 5,000-10,000 IU a day for a short time, then maintenance. Each extra 1,000 IU/day raises the level ~5-10 ng/mL over 2-3 months. 1,000 IU = 25 mcg.
entries.forms: Prefer D3 (cholecalciferol) over D2. Vegan D3 comes from lichen; most regular D3 from lanolin. One plain D3 softgel is usually all you need. Skip giant '100,000 IU' products. Look for a third-party seal (NSF Certified for Sport, USP Verified).
entries.timing: With the biggest meal of the day or any meal with fat. Time of day does not matter much. Daily.
entries.cycling: Retest 8-12 weeks after starting or changing the dose (some need 3-5 months). Once in range, test once or twice a year, same season. Do not go over 4,000 IU/day long term unless you are retesting 25-OH D and calcium.
entries.interactions: Take extra care and test often with sarcoidosis or other granulomatous disease, primary hyperparathyroidism, some lymphomas, or thiazide water pills. High-dose D plus calcium pills can raise kidney-stone risk. Low magnesium makes D work poorly. Pair with K2 (MK-7) at the same fatty meal.
entries.side_effects: Too much causes hypercalcemia: nausea or poor appetite, constipation, thirst and frequent urination, weakness, confusion, tiredness. Real toxicity usually appears above ~150 ng/mL; above 100 ng/mL is treated as too much from pills. Toxicity comes from pills, never from sun.
entries.contradictions: Low cut-off: the Short List (05.06.02) says under 30 ng/mL is low; Test First / 05.07.01 grade under 20 as deficient, 20-29 as insufficient and 30-100 as sufficient. Tate's target is 60-80 ng/mL; do not chase above 100.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.05 Test First; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.07.01 Vitamin D and K2; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol)
entries.why: D3 raises your blood level better and holds it longer.
entries.forms: Comes from plants and fungi. Use D3 instead.
entries.source: 05.07.01 Vitamin D and K2; 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.04 How to Read a Label

entries.name: Giant-dose vitamin D products (e.g. 100,000 IU)
entries.why: Doses this size are sold without testing, and above ~100 ng/mL there is no known benefit while the risk goes up. A 5,000 IU D3 is above the 4,000 IU limit and is only for use with a blood test and a retest plan.
entries.source: 05.07.01 Vitamin D and K2; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.06.04 How to Read a Label

entries.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-7, all-trans)
entries.verdict_text: Tier 1 alongside vitamin D; 'optional if diet and D level are fine'
entries.why: A low-risk add-on if you take vitamin D every day, especially at higher doses. It switches on osteocalcin and MGP. Pairing with D is a sensible team, not a proven combination; it is not proven to prevent heart attacks or fractures.
entries.dose_text: 90-200 mcg MK-7 a day (3-year bone trial 180 mcg; artery studies 360-720 mcg a day).
entries.forms: MK-7, ideally all-trans MK-7; it stays in the blood a long time, so one dose a day works. A third-party seal helps. Pick MK-7 unless you have a reason not to.
entries.timing: Once a day with the largest meal that has fat, along with vitamin D.
entries.interactions: Works against warfarin and can change INR. Do not start K2 on your own if you take warfarin; skip it unless a prescriber has set it up, and keep greens intake steady. It does not seem to interact much with DOACs (still check with a pharmacist).
entries.side_effects: Very safe for most people.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.04 How to Read a Label; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.07.01 Vitamin D and K2; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-4)
entries.why: It clears fast, so it needs much higher doses several times a day.
entries.source: 05.07.01 Vitamin D and K2; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
entries.why: Worth taking if you are in a risk group: vegan or little animal food, over 50-60, on metformin or acid reducers, gut conditions or weight-loss surgery, pernicious anemia, heavy alcohol. For everyone else a varied diet usually covers it. A shortage builds slowly and nerve damage can be permanent.
entries.dose_text: Maintenance 500-1,000 mcg a day; fix a shortage 1,000-2,000 mcg a day orally. Vegans: daily, or a high dose weekly. Injection is commonly 1,000 mcg: a few shots close together, then monthly. Adult need is 2.4 mcg/day. No known upper limit, but higher doses buy nothing once you are replete.
entries.forms: Any of the four forms works for most people. Cyanocobalamin is the cheapest and most stable and is the default (unnamed 'Vitamin B12' is usually cyanocobalamin). Methylcobalamin is a reasonable pick with MTHFR, nerve symptoms or preference, but a 'methylated' label is not proof of a better result. Hydroxocobalamin is often chosen for injections. Sublingual is about the same as swallowed. Blends of all four are 'fine, but not needed'. B12 shots for energy when your level is fine do not give you energy.
entries.timing: Daily (vegans: daily or a high dose weekly).
entries.cycling: MMA usually drops within 4-8 weeks; retest B12 and homocysteine ~8-12 weeks after starting. On metformin or acid reducers, test once a year.
entries.interactions: Metformin, PPIs and H2 blockers lower B12. Nitrous oxide inactivates B12. Never treat anemia or high MCV with folate alone: check B12 first. Test B12, folate and homocysteine as a set.
entries.side_effects: Very safe; rare mild stomach upset; rare allergy to the shot. With Leber's disease, avoid cyanocobalamin. Numbness or tingling, balance trouble, memory loss or confusion, or a sore smooth red tongue need medical care, not home pills.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.05 Test First; 05.07.02 Vitamin B12; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Folic acid
entries.why: Use it to fix a real shortage or a high homocysteine, not as a heart shield. Most healthy people who eat beans, greens and fortified grains get enough. In pregnancy, folate is not optional.
entries.dose_text: Standard 400-800 mcg a day; pregnancy 400 mcg a day; homocysteine trials 0.5-5 mg a day. 400 mcg folic acid ≈ 680 mcg DFE.
entries.forms: Synthetic; needs DHFR then MTHFR conversion. For most people folic acid works fine.
entries.timing: Pregnancy: start at least a month before trying to conceive and continue through at least the first three months.
entries.cycling: Retest homocysteine 8-12 weeks after starting; RBC folate after a few months.
entries.interactions: Can hide a B12 shortage (fixes the anemia while nerve damage progresses), so check B12 before or with high-dose folate and always pair it with B12. With methotrexate, the prescriber adds folic or folinic acid. It can lower phenytoin and other seizure-drug levels; check with a pharmacist.
entries.side_effects: The health meaning of unmetabolized folic acid at large amounts is not settled.
entries.contradictions: 05.07.03 gives 400-800 mcg a day as standard, while its quick summary says 'folic acid or methylfolate, 400 to 1,000 mcg'. The homocysteine goal is given as under 7 (S1647) and as under 7-9 umol/L (S1648).
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.05 Test First; 05.07.03 Folate, Folic Acid and Methylfolate; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Methylfolate (5-MTHF / L-methylfolate)
entries.verdict_text: 'Ready to use. Costs more. Useful if conversion is slow.'
entries.why: A reasonable pick if an MTHFR variant slows conversion, homocysteine stays high on folic acid, or you want to avoid unmetabolized folic acid.
entries.dose_text: 400-1,000 mcg a day (MTHFR plan: with B12 500-1,000 mcg/day).
entries.cycling: Retest homocysteine 8-12 weeks after starting.
entries.interactions: Pair with B12. Measure homocysteine first: if it is under 7 umol/L and you carry TT, there is nothing to treat.
entries.side_effects: Some feel wired, jittery or agitated on high doses (evidence for 'overmethylation' is thin). If that happens, lower the dose.
entries.source: 05.07.03 Folate, Folic Acid and Methylfolate; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Folinic acid
entries.why: It also works for MTHFR. Prescribers use it with methotrexate.
entries.dose_text: No standalone dose given (with methotrexate, the prescriber sets the dose; do not guess).
entries.source: 05.07.03 Folate, Folic Acid and Methylfolate; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Riboflavin (vitamin B2)
entries.verdict_text: 'An underused tool' for MTHFR C677T TT
entries.why: It lowers homocysteine in C677T TT carriers and is needed with zinc to activate B6. A shortage is uncommon if you eat dairy or meat; it is more likely in vegans with few fortified foods.
entries.dose_text: Not stated (B-complex amounts are usually well above the need).
entries.side_effects: Bright yellow urine (harmless).
entries.source: 05.07.03 Folate, Folic Acid and Methylfolate; 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Betaine (TMG, trimethylglycine)
entries.why: An add-on in the MTHFR plan when homocysteine stays high despite methylfolate and B12.
entries.dose_text: 1-3 g a day.
entries.source: 05.07.03 Folate, Folic Acid and Methylfolate; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: B complex
entries.verdict_text: 'Makes sense for people with a real reason'
entries.why: B vitamins give energy only if you were short. It makes sense for vegans or very restricted diets, very-low-calorie diets, older adults, heavy drinkers, weight-loss surgery or gut conditions, metformin or acid reducers, and high homocysteine. Otherwise you likely get enough from food.
entries.dose_text: Close to what you need, not 100 times more.
entries.forms: Forms listed (methylfolate, methylcobalamin); USP Verified or NSF Certified for Sport; note it may contain biotin. Avoid B vitamins at 10× RDA or more.
entries.interactions: May contain biotin: stop 48-72 h before blood tests. Add up B6 across all products.
entries.side_effects: Bright yellow urine is harmless riboflavin, a sign you took more than you need.
entries.source: 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Thiamine (vitamin B1)
entries.verdict_text: Worth knowing if you are a heavy drinker, post-surgery or on a restricted diet
entries.why: Heavy drinking is the top cause of low thiamine. Weight-loss surgery, long vomiting or diarrhea, loop diuretics and low magnesium also lower it. Otherwise food covers it.
entries.dose_text: Need is ~1.1-1.2 mg a day. No supplement dose is given.
entries.forms: Thiamine HCl or mononitrate are the usual forms. Benfotiamine and sulbutiamine are fat-soluble and enter tissue better; benfotiamine is used for diabetic nerve pain.
entries.interactions: Needs magnesium to work.
entries.side_effects: Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, poor balance, odd eye movements) is an emergency that needs IV thiamine in hospital.
entries.source: 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)
entries.verdict_text: 'Just filler. It does no harm and no good.'
entries.why: A true B5 shortage is very rare. Claims for acne, 'adrenal fatigue' and stress are not backed by good studies.
entries.side_effects: High doses cause diarrhea or upset stomach.
entries.source: 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Niacin (nicotinic acid), high-dose
entries.verdict_text: 'Do not try it on your own'
entries.why: Do not take high-dose niacin on your own for cholesterol or anything else. In AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE, niacin added to statins did not cut heart attacks or strokes. It lowers Lp(a) by ~20-30% with no proof of benefit. Multivitamin or B-complex amounts are fine.
entries.dose_text: Need ~14-16 mg a day. Cholesterol doses of 1,000-3,000 mg a day (H4: 1,000-2,000 mg) are prescription-drug territory, with liver and sugar monitoring.
entries.forms: Sustained-release or 'slow release' forms carry the highest liver risk. Skip 'flush-free' products.
entries.interactions: If liver tests rise, stop and retest.
entries.side_effects: Flush at ~30-50 mg+ of nicotinic acid (red, warm, itchy; starts in 15-30 minutes, fades in ~1 hour; not dangerous). At high doses: liver injury, higher glucose/HbA1c, higher uric acid (gout), lower SHBG, stomach upset, low BP, dizziness.
entries.contradictions: 05.07.04 gives cholesterol doses of 1,000-3,000 mg a day; 05.12.04 says 1,000-2,000 mg a day.
entries.source: 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Niacinamide (nicotinamide)
entries.verdict_text: 'No flush. It does not change cholesterol.'
entries.why: A B3 form with no flush that does nothing for cholesterol. The vault gives no other verdict or dose.
entries.source: 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet; 05.13.01 NAD Boosters - NMN and NR

entries.name: Inositol hexanicotinate ('flush-free' / 'no-flush' niacin)
entries.why: Little of it turns into usable niacin, so it does little, including for cholesterol. It is not a safer way to get the same effect.
entries.source: 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine / P5P)
entries.verdict_text: 'Helpful, until the dose is too high'; stop if tingling or numbness
entries.why: Use food first, then a low dose in a B complex or multivitamin. Take 25-50 mg only to correct a proven low level, then retest. More is clearly not better: long high doses can cause nerve damage.
entries.dose_text: Need ~1.3-1.7 mg a day; fix a real shortage with 25-50 mg a day.
entries.forms: Pyridoxine HCl (usual) or P5P (active form). Neuropathy has been reported with both.
entries.interactions: Most overdose is accidental stacking: B complex + multivitamin + pre-workout + recovery drink + standalone B6. Add up B6 from every product.
entries.side_effects: Peripheral neuropathy (tingling, numbness, burning, pain in hands and feet, balance trouble), usually reversible if stopped early. Cases are reported below 100 mg with long use. If tingling appears, stop B6 and tell your clinician.
entries.contradictions: Upper limit: US 100 mg a day; Europe's food safety agency 12 mg a day.
entries.source: 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Biotin (vitamin B7)
entries.why: A true shortage is very rare (long-term raw egg white, certain seizure drugs, rare disorders). There is no good proof that extra biotin grows hair or strengthens nails. The main risk is lab interference: it falsifies thyroid, hormone and troponin tests.
entries.dose_text: Need is ~30 mcg a day. Bottles often hold 5,000-10,000 mcg (5-10 mg) or more; 5 mg or more can interfere with tests.
entries.timing: Stop at least 3 days (72 h) before any blood draw, and longer with 100 mg+. Tell the lab or ER you take it. Check multivitamins, B complexes, 'energy' blends and hair products for hidden biotin. Redo surprising results after stopping.
entries.interactions: Lab effects: falsely low TSH and high free T4/T3 (looks like an overactive thyroid); falsely high testosterone; may affect cortisol, estradiol, progesterone, LH, FSH, prolactin, DHEA-S, IGF-1, SHBG, B12 and folate; falsely low troponin (FDA warning).
entries.contradictions: Pre-test stop window: 05.06.05 and 05.14.06 say at least 3 days (72 hours); the B complex/multivitamin chapters (05.07.04, 05.07.07) and 05.11.05 say 48-72 hours.
entries.source: 05.06.05 Test First; 05.07.04 B Complex, Niacin, B6 and Biotin; 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.11.05 DHEA and Pregnenolone; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
entries.verdict_text: Gap filler — 'cheap and low risk at ordinary doses'
entries.why: A gap filler for people eating almost no produce, heavy drinkers, smokers, dialysis, healing from surgery or burns, and people under extreme physical stress. It did not lower colds in the general public ('expensive urine'), though daily use may shorten colds a little. It is the one supplement where more is clearly not better.
entries.dose_text: RDA: men 90 mg, women 75 mg, smokers +35 mg. Fill the blood tank with 200-500 mg a day. Fix a true deficiency with 300-1,000 mg a day for a short stretch. Cold studies used 200 mg+ every day. As a collagen co-factor, ~50 mg with the tendon collagen dose.
entries.forms: Plain ascorbic acid is preferred. Mineral ascorbates (buffered) are easier on a sensitive stomach but add sodium or calcium at big doses. Acerola or food-based C is often a small amount per capsule. Chewables can wear enamel. Gummies often hold less than the label says. Fizzy tablets can carry a lot of sodium.
entries.timing: Split any dose over 500 mg into 2-3. Any time of day; with food is gentler. Take with an iron-rich meal or iron pill if you need iron. Keep high doses away from training.
entries.interactions: Skip high doses with a past calcium-oxalate stone or kidney disease. With hemochromatosis or high ferritin, skip vitamin C pills with meals. With cancer treatment, check with an oncology pharmacist. Birth control lowers levels. Regular aspirin raises urinary loss. It roughly doubles non-heme iron absorption. It can interfere with some finger-stick glucose meters, stool occult blood tests and some lab methods. IV vitamin C drips can burst red blood cells in G6PD deficiency: do not get one.
entries.side_effects: Above the UL: diarrhea, gas, cramps. Men taking 1,000 mg a day or more had more kidney stones. 1,000 mg pills of C and E around workouts may blunt training gains.
entries.source: 05.07.05 Vitamin C; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.14.03 Collagen; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Liposomal vitamin C
entries.why: It has not been shown to improve health beyond plain ascorbic acid, and it costs a lot more. Plain split doses get most of the same gain.
entries.source: 05.07.05 Vitamin C; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin A (preformed retinol)
entries.verdict_text: 'Get A and E from food first'; only with a clear reason
entries.why: Take vitamin A only with a clear reason, like a proven low result or fat malabsorption. It is not needed if you eat eggs, dairy and orange or green vegetables. Long-term excess harms the liver and bones and causes birth defects.
entries.dose_text: RDA men 900 mcg RAE a day, women 700 mcg RAE. UL 3,000 mcg RAE (10,000 IU) of preformed A, counting supplements, liver and cod liver oil.
entries.timing: With fat-containing food. If you eat liver, once a week is plenty; count it as your vitamin A for the week.
entries.interactions: Pregnancy or trying to conceive: no high-dose A pills; many agencies advise avoiding liver and cod liver oil. Don't mix with vitamin-A-derived prescription acne drugs. Add up A across all labels (multivitamin, hair gummies, organ capsules). Keep away from children.
entries.side_effects: Toxicity: headache, dry flaking skin, cracked lips, hair loss, high liver enzymes, bone and joint pain. A large single dose causes nausea, dizziness and a pounding headache. Severe headache with vision changes needs a doctor right away. Chronic high intake weakens bones.
entries.source: 05.07.06 Vitamins A and E; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Beta-carotene pills (isolated high-dose)
entries.why: If you smoke or quit recently, do not take isolated high-dose beta-carotene, whatever your genes say: in ATBC and CARET it raised lung cancer in smokers and asbestos workers. Beta-carotene from food is fine and self-limiting.
entries.interactions: Do not take a multivitamin high in beta-carotene if you smoke.
entries.side_effects: Food excess only causes harmless orange skin (carotenodermia).
entries.source: 05.07.06 Vitamins A and E; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vitamin E (natural d-alpha-tocopherol / mixed tocopherols)
entries.verdict_text: 'Large single pills are not worth the risk for most people'
entries.why: Food first. A multivitamin dose near the RDA is fine. Skip 400 IU+ pills unless you have a clear reason (mainly fat malabsorption). In SELECT, 400 IU a day raised prostate cancer, and it did not prevent heart disease.
entries.dose_text: RDA 15 mg a day alpha-tocopherol. UL 1,000 mg a day from supplements (≈1,500 IU natural). The 800 IU fatty-liver dose is a narrow, supervised case: do not start it on your own.
entries.forms: Natural d-alpha (RRR) absorbs better than synthetic dl-alpha. A mixed-tocopherol product is safer than a pure high-dose alpha pill, which can lower gamma-tocopherol. 1 mg natural ≈ 1.5 IU.
entries.timing: With a meal (fat). Skip high-dose C and E around workouts.
entries.interactions: Works against vitamin K and thins the blood mildly. If you take warfarin, aspirin or other thinners, have surgery coming or bruise easily, check with a pharmacist and watch INR. Fish oil and PUFA raise need.
entries.side_effects: Possible small rise in total deaths at 400 IU+ (disputed). High doses may blunt training adaptations.
entries.source: 05.07.06 Vitamins A and E; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione; 05.13.05 Alpha-Lipoic Acid, PQQ and Astaxanthin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Synthetic vitamin E (dl-alpha-tocopherol)
entries.why: 2 mg of synthetic equals 1 mg of natural, and natural absorbs better.
entries.source: 05.07.06 Vitamins A and E

entries.name: Tocotrienols
entries.why: Expensive supplements with big claims and thin human evidence. There is no proof they beat regular vitamin E.
entries.source: 05.07.06 Vitamins A and E

entries.name: Multivitamin
entries.why: A fair backup for restricted or low-calorie diets, vegans, older adults, pregnancy, poor absorption or weight-loss surgery, or a proven gap. For well-fed people it mostly makes expensive urine: COSMOS (>21,000 older adults) found no drop in cancer, heart events or deaths, and USPSTF calls the evidence insufficient.
entries.dose_text: One pill a day with doses near the RDA; avoid 10× RDA or more for B vitamins; don't double up with a second multi.
entries.forms: Iron-free version for most men and post-menopausal women unless a test says otherwise. Named forms (methylfolate, methylcobalamin, d-alpha E). Vitamin A mostly as beta-carotene or modest retinol. Third-party seal (NSF Certified for Sport, USP Verified, Informed Sport). Weak spots: tiny calcium and magnesium, low vitamin D, zero omega-3, magnesium oxide. Avoid 'mega' or 'extra strength', big blends with no amounts, and gummies if you want full minerals.
entries.timing: Once a day with a meal. Keep iron/calcium in a multi ~4 h from levothyroxine. Pause biotin-containing multis 48-72 h before a blood draw.
entries.cycling: Fix any measured low with a real dose and retest in ~3 months. Stop if tests show no shortfall and your diet is strong, you are over-stacking, or you get side effects.
entries.interactions: Warfarin: vitamin K content (keep intake steady). Levothyroxine: iron and calcium. Biotin: lab interference. Add totals across fortified foods, protein powder and hair pills (fat-soluble vitamins, iron, zinc, selenium). Iron versions are dangerous with HFE hemochromatosis.
entries.side_effects: Nausea (especially on an empty stomach), constipation or dark stools (iron), metallic taste. If a child swallows one, call poison control. Black tarry stools with blood or severe pain need a doctor fast.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.07.07 Multivitamins and Greens Powders; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Prenatal multivitamin (with folate)
entries.verdict_text: 'A real exception' — truly recommended in pregnancy or planning
entries.why: Standard care in pregnancy or when planning: provides folate (400 mcg folic acid from at least a month before conception through the first 3 months). Check that it contains iodine, since many lack it.
entries.interactions: Stay within pregnancy limits for vitamin A. Pregnant or nursing women are advised 150 mcg iodine a day from a supplement.
entries.source: 05.06.06 Safety; 05.07.03 Folate, Folic Acid and Methylfolate; 05.07.07 Multivitamins and Greens Powders; 05.08.04 Iodine and Selenium; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 'Men's', 'women's' and '50+' multivitamin formulas
entries.why: Women's versions often have more iron; men's and 50+ versions often skip it. Over 50, check B12. Vegans should look for B12, zinc and iodine.
entries.source: 05.07.07 Multivitamins and Greens Powders

entries.name: Greens powders
entries.verdict_text: 'Little good evidence'; 'a small extra, not a health plan'
entries.why: Treat it as a small convenience, not a health treatment. Vegetables win on almost every count. It is better than nothing only for someone who won't eat vegetables but will drink a shake. Named ingredients are usually far below studied doses, and it is not an immune tool.
entries.forms: If used: every ingredient and amount listed, no proprietary blend, third-party tested (NSF/USP or a published certificate of analysis). Don't use it to replace a vegetable meal.
entries.interactions: Can be high in vitamin K, so skip it if you take a blood thinner without checking first. May contain caffeine or adaptogens.
entries.side_effects: Heavy metals (spirulina and chlorella are higher risk); gas or loose stools at the start.
entries.source: 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.07.07 Multivitamins and Greens Powders; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Proprietary-blend multis and greens
entries.verdict_text: 'Almost never a clinical dose of anything'
entries.why: The blend hides each amount, so you rarely get a clinical dose of anything.
entries.source: 05.07.07 Multivitamins and Greens Powders; 05.06.03 Buying Supplements

entries.name: Magnesium (general)
entries.verdict_text: Tier 1, if your diet is low
entries.why: Fixes a real shortage that is common. Most of the benefit shows up in people who start low: modest help for sleep (tens of minutes), blood sugar and blood pressure (a few points). Evidence for cramps is weak to mixed.
entries.dose_text: 200-400 mg elemental a day. Start at 200 mg elemental (glycinate) in the evening and go up toward 400 mg only if needed and your gut allows; split larger doses. RDA women ~310-320 mg, men 400-420 mg. A 1,000 mg glycinate capsule may hold only ~100-140 mg elemental.
entries.forms: Glycinate (best all-round, gentle, evening); citrate (well absorbed, mildly laxative); malate (fine, well absorbed). Not oxide for fixing a shortage. Skip vague 'magnesium complex' or blend labels. Read the label for elemental magnesium and look for a third-party seal.
entries.timing: Glycinate in the evening fits sleep; split morning and evening if taking more; take with food if your stomach is sensitive. Keep ≥2 h from bisphosphonates and tetracyclines. Take a fluoroquinolone ≥2 h before or 4-6 h after magnesium. Keep ~4 h from thyroid medicine.
entries.cycling: Give it 8-12 weeks, then retest RBC magnesium. Stop if your level is fine and you feel no change.
entries.interactions: With weak kidneys it can build up to a dangerous level: avoid with significant kidney disease unless a specialist watches levels. It adds to blood-pressure pills. PPIs and diuretics drain magnesium. You need it to activate vitamin D, and low magnesium can keep potassium and calcium from correcting.
entries.side_effects: Loose stools or diarrhea (most with oxide, citrate and large single doses). Too much: severe diarrhea, low blood pressure, drowsiness, muscle weakness, slow heartbeat. Stop and get help.
entries.contradictions: 05.06.02 (S1606) gives 200-400 mg elemental a day but also a supplement upper limit of 350 mg/day, and the vault 'does not reconcile the two figures' (05.10.02 states both as well).
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.04 How to Read a Label; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.08.01 Magnesium; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Magnesium glycinate (bisglycinate)
entries.why: Gentle, well absorbed and calming; the usual pick for sleep and for fixing a shortage.
entries.dose_text: Start ~200 mg elemental in the evening; 200-400 mg elemental a day; supplement UL 350 mg.
entries.timing: Evening.
entries.interactions: Same spacing as magnesium (antibiotics, bisphosphonates, thyroid medicine); kidney disease caution.
entries.contradictions: The 200-400 mg range sits above the 350 mg supplement UL; the vault does not reconcile the two (S1606).
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Magnesium citrate
entries.why: Well absorbed and acceptable for fixing a shortage. Pick it if you are constipated; it is a poor pick if your stools are already loose.
entries.dose_text: As for magnesium: 200-400 mg elemental; supplement UL 350 mg.
entries.side_effects: Diarrhea is more common.
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Magnesium malate
entries.why: Acceptable for fixing a shortage. It is marketed as a daytime form, but there is no strong proof it works differently.
entries.dose_text: As for magnesium: 200-400 mg elemental; supplement UL 350 mg.
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Magnesium L-threonate
entries.why: Sold for the brain. It is costly, and each capsule holds little actual magnesium.
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Magnesium taurate
entries.why: Sold for heart and blood pressure, but there is little direct human evidence for that claim.
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium

entries.name: Magnesium chloride (oral)
entries.verdict_text: Absorbed fairly well; can upset the stomach
entries.why: The oral form is absorbed fairly well but can upset the stomach.
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium

entries.name: Topical magnesium (oils, sprays, bath salts)
entries.verdict_text: Weak proof that they raise your levels
entries.why: Skin sprays, oils and bath salts have weak proof that they raise your levels.
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium

entries.name: Magnesium oxide
entries.why: Only about 4-15% is absorbed, so it is a poor way to fix a shortage. It mostly acts as a laxative. Cheap 'complex' or blend labels are often mostly oxide, used to make the milligram number look big.
entries.side_effects: Causes the most diarrhea of the forms.
entries.source: 05.08.01 Magnesium; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.04 How to Read a Label; 05.07.07 Multivitamins and Greens Powders; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Zinc
entries.verdict_text: 'Fixes a shortage'; it will not boost T, colds or skin if you have enough
entries.why: Zinc fixes a shortage. It is not a booster for people who have enough. If you eat meat, shellfish or dairy most days, you probably do not need a pill. It raises testosterone only if you are low.
entries.dose_text: 15-30 mg elemental a day for 8-12 weeks, then retest. General top-up: 15 mg (picolinate, citrate or glycinate) with dinner. Targets: men ~11 mg, women 8 mg. Do not megadose.
entries.forms: Picolinate, citrate and glycinate are well absorbed (pick one to fix a shortage); gluconate is also well absorbed. Not oxide.
entries.timing: With a meal (dinner) to avoid nausea. Take iron and calcium pills at a different time of day. Keep away from high-phytate meals. Take tetracycline or fluoroquinolone antibiotics ≥2 h before or 4-6 h after zinc.
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks, then retest (and retest testosterone at 8-12 weeks if that was the reason).
entries.interactions: Competes with iron and calcium; phytates bind it. Add up zinc from multivitamins, greens, immune blends and T formulas. Long-term high zinc drains copper: add 1-2 mg copper per 15-30 mg zinc for long-term use. Draw the test in the morning, fasting, before the day's dose, in a trace-element tube; inflammation and illness lower zinc.
entries.side_effects: Nausea on an empty stomach; metal taste. Over 40 mg a day for months drains copper (anemia, weakened immunity, nerve problems).
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.08.02 Zinc and Copper; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Zinc oxide (oral)
entries.verdict_text: 'Do not use it to fix a shortage'
entries.why: Cheap and poorly absorbed.
entries.source: 05.08.02 Zinc and Copper

entries.name: Zinc lozenges (acetate / gluconate) for colds
entries.verdict_text: 'Can shorten colds modestly' — 'Start early or skip them'
entries.why: The one cold supplement with a real mechanism and some real results: it may cut a cold by a day or so (results mixed). There is no good evidence that daily use without symptoms prevents colds.
entries.dose_text: About 75 mg elemental zinc a day or more, spread across several lozenges, for a few days. Read the elemental amount on the label.
entries.forms: Acetate (best studied) or gluconate lozenges that dissolve in the mouth. Lozenges with citric or tartaric acid may not work. Not swallowed pills.
entries.timing: Start within about a day of the first symptoms; let each lozenge dissolve slowly without chewing.
entries.cycling: A short burst, not a habit: stop when the cold is gone (within about a week or two).
entries.interactions: Zinc can bind some antibiotics and bone medicines; check with a pharmacist. Take iron and calcium at a different time.
entries.side_effects: Bad taste and nausea are common (food can ease the nausea). About 40 mg/day or more over time can drain copper.
entries.contradictions: The ~75 mg/day lozenge dose is above the ~40 mg long-term UL; the vault treats it as a short burst only.
entries.source: 05.08.02 Zinc and Copper; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Zinc nasal sprays / gels / swabs
entries.why: Linked to lasting loss of smell; the FDA has warned about them.
entries.source: 05.08.02 Zinc and Copper; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Copper
entries.why: If you take zinc for many months, add copper to prevent a low copper level. Also relevant after gastric bypass, celiac or Crohn's. Do not take big copper doses on your own.
entries.dose_text: 1-2 mg copper per 15-30 mg zinc. Daily target ~0.9 mg.
entries.interactions: High zinc is the most common cause of low copper in people who take supplements. Copper rises with inflammation, pregnancy and estrogen or birth control, so check hs-CRP before cutting copper over one high number. Very low ceruloplasmin with liver or nerve symptoms in a young person may mean Wilson disease: get care fast.
entries.side_effects: Deficiency signs: anemia that does not respond to iron, low white cells, numbness, tingling, trouble walking.
entries.source: 05.08.02 Zinc and Copper; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Iron
entries.verdict_text: 'Only when labs show a shortage' — 'Do not take iron on a guess'
entries.why: Take iron only when labs show a shortage, not for tiredness alone. Your body cannot get rid of extra. Main groups: women with periods, pregnancy, endurance athletes, blood donors, low-meat eaters, gut trouble. Men and post-menopausal women rarely need it; if they are low, check for hidden blood loss.
entries.dose_text: Alternate-day dosing, 60-120 mg elemental. A ferrous sulfate 325 mg tablet ≈ 65 mg elemental. RDA ~8 mg for men and post-menopausal women, ~18 mg for women 19-50. Adult UL 45 mg a day from supplements unless a clinician is treating a shortage.
entries.forms: Ferrous sulfate works but upsets the stomach most. Bisglycinate is gentler (a good pick if sulfate gives you trouble). Gluconate is often easier on the stomach. IV iron is given in clinic if you cannot absorb or tolerate pills.
entries.timing: Every other day, on an empty stomach if tolerated, with vitamin C. Keep coffee, tea, calcium, dairy and acid reducers 1-2 h away (calcium ≥2 h). Not in the few hours after a hard workout. Keep ~4 h from levothyroxine.
entries.cycling: Retest ferritin, TSAT and hemoglobin at 8-12 weeks. Continue 3-6 months after ferritin normalizes, then stop and move to a food plan. Do not keep taking it 'just in case'.
entries.interactions: Blocks levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and levodopa. Competes with zinc and manganese. Don't stack on a multivitamin with iron. Do not take it without labs if you are a man, post-menopausal, have a family history of hemochromatosis, high ferritin with TSAT ≥45%, or unexplained high liver enzymes or blood sugar. With HFE hemochromatosis, stop iron pills and iron multivitamins.
entries.side_effects: Constipation, nausea, stomach pain; dark or black stools are normal. Black, tarry, sticky stools with stomach pain can mean bleeding: see a doctor fast. Serious poisoning risk for small children, so lock it away.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.05 Test First; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.08.03 Iron; 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.07.07 Multivitamins and Greens Powders; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Iodine
entries.verdict_text: Test before supplementing; for most people, no pill
entries.why: Iodized salt plus some dairy and seafood covers it for most people. Pregnant and nursing women are the exception. Too much causes thyroid disease. A 150 mcg iodine supplement is safer than sea moss if you eat no dairy, fish or iodized salt.
entries.dose_text: Adults ~150 mcg a day (pregnancy 220 mcg, nursing 290 mcg). Pregnant or nursing: 150 mcg a day from a supplement (check the prenatal label; many lack iodine).
entries.timing: Daily (the body holds little reserve).
entries.cycling: Retest in 8-12 weeks if supplementing.
entries.interactions: Hidden sources: iodine contrast dye, amiodarone, multivitamins or prenatals stacked with kelp. Pair with selenium: high iodine with low selenium can injure the thyroid. Avoid extra iodine from kelp while using selenium for Hashimoto's.
entries.side_effects: U-shaped risk: excess can cause hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism or autoimmune thyroid flares. A racing heart, shakiness, weight loss or neck swelling after kelp or iodine means stop and get TSH checked fast.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.08.04 Iodine and Selenium; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Kelp pills / 'thyroid support' blends
entries.verdict_text: 'Do not treat kelp as a gentle supplement'
entries.why: One serving can deliver milligrams of iodine, enough to pass the ~1,100 mcg upper limit in one dose. Skip kelp pills and megadose iodine plans.
entries.source: 05.08.04 Iodine and Selenium; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Megadose iodine plans (milligrams a day)
entries.why: Do not follow one without monitoring. Especially risky with Hashimoto's or a lumpy thyroid.
entries.source: 05.08.04 Iodine and Selenium

entries.name: Selenium (selenomethionine / selenium yeast)
entries.verdict_text: 'Test before you take one'; 'does not replace thyroid medicine'
entries.why: If you eat seafood, eggs or a few Brazil nuts a week, you probably don't need it. It helps most if you are low, especially with positive TPO antibodies (~200 mcg lowered antibodies in trials). If your level is already 90-125 mcg/L, a pill will not add benefit; it only adds risk.
entries.dose_text: Typical 100-200 mcg a day; Hashimoto's trials used ~200 mcg a day selenomethionine. Targets: adults 55 mcg, pregnancy 60, nursing 70. Count Brazil nuts and multivitamins in the total.
entries.forms: Selenomethionine or selenium yeast is best absorbed; selenite and selenate are other forms. Label should show actual mcg per serving and an NSF/USP seal.
entries.cycling: Antibody effect is strongest at 3-6 months; T3 effects take 8-12 weeks or longer. Recheck antibodies at 3-6 months and thyroid hormones at 8-12 weeks.
entries.interactions: Selenium is a helper, not a substitute for levothyroxine. Balance with iodine. Myo-inositol 600 mg + selenium 83 mcg twice daily lowered TPO antibodies more than selenium alone in some studies. Hidden sources: Brazil nuts, multivitamins, thyroid blends, hair-skin-nails pills.
entries.side_effects: Selenosis: hair loss or brittle hair, brittle nails, garlic breath, stomach upset, numbness or tingling. Stop and retest. Years of 200 mcg in replete people showed no cancer prevention, and some trials found higher type 2 diabetes risk.
entries.source: 05.08.04 Iodine and Selenium; 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Brazil nuts (as a selenium source)
entries.verdict_text: 'One or two a few times a week is often enough'
entries.why: Each nut holds ~68-91 mcg or more of selenium. One or two a day is the most to aim for; a handful a day can push you past the safe limit.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.08.04 Iodine and Selenium; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Calcium (carbonate / citrate)
entries.verdict_text: Tier 2 — food first; a pill only to close a real gap
entries.why: Most people who eat dairy or fortified foods do not need a calcium pill. Use a supplement only to close a real gap (little or no dairy, post-menopausal women, older adults, gut problems, long-term steroids), with meals and in small doses. Fracture-prevention results are small and mixed, and extra is not always better.
entries.dose_text: Total target ~1,000-1,200 mg a day from food plus pills. The pill covers only the gap, often 300-600 mg a day, no more than ~500 mg at once (e.g. 600 mg → 300 mg twice daily with food). '1,250 mg calcium carbonate' may hold ~500 mg elemental.
entries.forms: Carbonate (~40% calcium) is the cheapest but needs a meal. Citrate (~21%) absorbs with or without food and is the better pick with acid blockers, stomach surgery or carbonate upset.
entries.timing: With lunch or dinner (carbonate requires a meal); take other pills at breakfast or bed. Split if over 500 mg. Iron ≥2 h apart. Wait ~4 h after levothyroxine. Take bisphosphonates first thing with plain water and keep calcium a couple of hours away.
entries.cycling: Retest after a few months of a new routine, then yearly.
entries.interactions: Blocks thyroid pills (~4 h apart). Competes with iron, zinc and magnesium, so space them out. Thiazides plus extra calcium and D can push calcium too high, and lithium can raise calcium. For tetracyclines and quinolones, ask a pharmacist for the gap.
entries.side_effects: Carbonate causes gas, bloating and constipation. Hypercalcemia: thirst, tiredness, constipation, nausea, frequent urination; very high levels cause confusion and rhythm problems. Pills are mixed for heart risk ('slightly more heart attacks' in some studies), so no big doses. High-dose calcium with D raised stone risk in stone-prone people.
entries.contradictions: Upper limit is ~2,500 mg a day up to age 50 and ~2,000 mg a day after 50 (total from all sources).
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.08.05 Calcium; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Algae calcium / bone meal
entries.verdict_text: Not clearly better; can carry lead
entries.why: Not clearly better than carbonate or citrate. Bone meal and some natural sources can carry lead; if used, pick a third-party tested product (USP Verified).
entries.source: 05.08.05 Calcium

entries.name: Chewable antacids as a calcium source
entries.why: Large daily amounts of calcium-carbonate antacids can cause high blood calcium and kidney harm, so count them.
entries.source: 05.08.05 Calcium

entries.name: Electrolyte mixes
entries.verdict_text: Tier 1, if you sweat a lot or eat very low-carb
entries.why: Useful for long or hard sessions (especially in heat), heavy or salty sweaters, and low-carb, keto or very-low-calorie diets. Most people do not need one: under an hour in normal weather with regular meals, water and food are enough. They do not give energy or burn fat. Evidence is best for sodium.
entries.dose_text: Useful mix per serving: sodium 300-1,000 mg, potassium ~150-300 mg, magnesium ~50-100 mg. Long or hot sessions: ~300-700 mg sodium per hour. Rehydration: 500-700 mg sodium + 80-150 mg potassium per 500-750 mL water.
entries.forms: Read the label for milligrams; a vague 'electrolyte blend' with no amounts is a red flag. Many drinks are mostly sugar. Citrate or chloride are fine (citrate is gentler); magnesium as glycinate or citrate beats oxide. Check for caffeine. 'Hydration multipliers' is marketing. Salt in water is the base of all of them, and cheap swaps work as well.
entries.timing: Sip through long (>1 h) or hot sessions rather than gulping at the end; ~500 mL in the 2-3 h before training; 180-360 mL every 15-20 minutes during long sessions.
test_first: basic metabolic panel (sodium, potassium, creatinine, eGFR) if new diet, symptoms or meds
entries.interactions: Do not add sodium or potassium on your own with high BP, heart failure or kidney disease. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing diuretics raise potassium. Tested athletes: NSF Certified for Sport or Informed Sport.
entries.side_effects: Plain water in excess causes hyponatremia (headache, nausea, bloating, confusion; seizure or collapse is an emergency). Drink to thirst and don't drink more than you sweat.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.08.06 Electrolytes - Sodium, Potassium and Electrolyte Mixes; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Sodium (salt, sodium citrate, salt tablets)
entries.verdict_text: 'A pinch of salt in water works too'
entries.why: Useful for long or hot sessions and for low-carb eaters, where plain water carries a hyponatremia risk. Do not use general low-salt advice if you are a hard-sweating athlete, but also do not salt blindly.
entries.dose_text: Long or hot sessions: ~300-700 mg sodium per hour with fluid (salty sweaters may need more); a carry drink with ~500-800 mg sodium per liter. Low-carb/keto: ~3-5 g (3,000-5,000 mg) sodium a day total. 1 level tsp salt ≈ 2,300 mg sodium.
entries.forms: Table salt is cheapest; sodium citrate is gentler on the stomach; a salty snack or broth is as good as a powder; plain sodium tablets suit long runs.
entries.timing: Sip across the workout. Short workouts: salt your lunch and drink to thirst.
entries.interactions: High BP, salt sensitivity or heart failure: don't freely add salt or a high-sodium mix. Kidney disease: don't add sodium on your own. Thiazides, SSRIs and NSAIDs affect sodium balance.
entries.side_effects: The scale can shift 1-2 lb overnight from salt and water.
entries.source: 05.08.06 Electrolytes - Sodium, Potassium and Electrolyte Mixes; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Potassium (pills, salt substitutes)
entries.why: Food is the best way to get potassium; OTC pills hold only ~99 mg. Do not add potassium pills to fix a cramp. Low potassium that won't rise often has low magnesium behind it.
entries.dose_text: Adults are advised ~2,600 mg (women) to 3,400 mg (men) a day, from food. Electrolyte mixes provide ~150-300 mg per serving.
entries.interactions: No potassium beyond food, including salt substitutes and mixes, with kidney disease or low eGFR, heart failure, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics, or diabetes with kidney trouble.
entries.side_effects: High blood potassium causes heart rhythm problems, even a stopped heart, sometimes with few warning signs.
entries.source: 05.08.06 Electrolytes - Sodium, Potassium and Electrolyte Mixes; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Boron
entries.verdict_text: 'Makes most sense with high SHBG after the basics are fixed'
entries.why: A cheap, plausible, minor lever on SHBG, not a way to make new testosterone. It fits men with high SHBG and free T low relative to total, after sleep, food, training, stress, zinc and vitamin D are fixed. It does nothing with normal or low SHBG, and women should not use it as a hormone tool.
entries.dose_text: Studied range 6-10 mg a day elemental; trial 6 mg a day for 4-8 weeks. Diet supplies ~1-2 mg a day. 30 or 40 mg only raises your risk.
entries.forms: Citrate, glycinate, calcium fructoborate and sodium borate; no form is better. Choose a single-ingredient product stating elemental boron, not a 'T matrix' blend.
entries.timing: With a meal.
entries.cycling: 4-8 week trial, then retest; stop if SHBG and free T didn't move. Don't start a week before an important test.
entries.interactions: Avoid with kidney disease, pregnancy or trying to conceive, or a hormone-sensitive condition. Ask a pharmacist about kidney-cleared medicines.
entries.side_effects: Very high doses cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache and skin problems.
entries.contradictions: The main evidence is one study of 8 men taking 10 mg/day for one week. 05.11.06 calls it 'far too small to trust' and 05.11.01 'a small and unproven SHBG effect', while 05.08.07 calls boron a 'cheap, plausible, minor lever'.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Manganese (stand-alone pills)
entries.verdict_text: Skip stand-alone pills unless a lab test points to one
entries.why: The real risk with manganese is too much: manganism causes tremor, stiffness and trouble walking. The small amount in a multivitamin is fine.
entries.dose_text: AI ~2.3 mg a day (men), 1.8 mg (women).
test_first: whole-blood manganese (only with exposure or liver trouble)
entries.interactions: Competes with iron; low iron means more manganese is absorbed.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Molybdenum (stand-alone pills)
entries.verdict_text: Not needed as a pill without a lab test and a clear reason
entries.why: Deficiency is extremely rare. Very high intakes can interfere with copper and may raise uric acid.
entries.dose_text: About 45 mcg a day.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Silicon (orthosilicic acid, horsetail, bamboo extract)
entries.why: No strong proof that silicon pills prevent fractures or fix thinning hair: at most a low-risk experiment, not a bone plan. Plant extracts such as horsetail vary in content, so skip them.
entries.dose_text: Diet provides ~20-50 mg a day; no recommended amount.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Lithium orotate (low-dose)
entries.why: There are no good trials for mood, memory or aging, and long-term safety is not well studied. Never self-treat with prescription lithium. For low mood, anxiety or racing thoughts, see someone who can treat them.
entries.dose_text: Supplements often provide ~1-5 mg lithium, some higher.
entries.interactions: Thiazides, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors can raise lithium levels. It can raise blood calcium.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Vanadium (vanadyl sulfate)
entries.verdict_text: 'You do not need any of these as pills'
entries.why: Sold for blood sugar; human evidence is weak and it can upset the stomach.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals

entries.name: Cobalt (pills)
entries.verdict_text: 'You do not need any of these as pills'
entries.why: Cobalt is only needed as part of vitamin B12.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals

entries.name: Nickel (pills)
entries.verdict_text: 'You do not need any of these as pills'
entries.why: Not needed as a pill.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals

entries.name: Trace mineral drops ('72 trace minerals', ionic, ocean minerals)
entries.why: Amounts are often unclear, doses are microgram-tiny, they can carry lead or arsenic, and there are no good trials. They can be high in sodium. They are not a way to fill gaps: test and fix the one truly low mineral at a real dose.
entries.source: 05.08.07 Boron and Other Trace Minerals; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Creatine monohydrate
entries.verdict_text: Tier 1 foundation — 'one of the few that reliably works'
entries.why: A proven performance tool for anyone who lifts: ~0.82 kg extra fat-free mass with training (older lifters ~1.4 kg). Vegetarians, vegans, lifters, older adults who train and larger people gain most. Women get the same gains at the same dose. It may also give small brain benefits when you are short on sleep or older.
entries.dose_text: 3-5 g a day, every day including rest days. Larger or very muscular people: 5-10 g a day ('Tate takes a big scoop, about 5 to 10 grams a day'). Optional loading: 20 g a day split into four 5 g doses for 5-7 days, then 5 g a day; without loading, muscles fill in 3-4 weeks.
entries.forms: Creatine monohydrate is the one to buy: most studied and cheapest. Fancier forms cost more and do not work better. Look for a tested raw material, NSF Certified for Sport or Informed Sport, no proprietary blend; it should be an off-white powder that mixes fully.
entries.timing: Barely matters; take it when you will remember. There may be a tiny edge right after a workout with carbs and protein. With or without food.
entries.cycling: No cycling needed; keep taking it, since benefits grow past 12 weeks. Low responders: stop if nothing after 8-12 weeks.
entries.interactions: Kidney disease: skip it unless a kidney specialist says yes. Take care combining with kidney-hard drugs if your kidneys are already weak. Pregnancy or nursing: the safe choice is to wait until after.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset with loading or high doses (split the dose or skip loading). Early weight gain of a pound or two is water inside the muscle, not fat. It nudges creatinine up, which is not kidney damage: pause 1-2 weeks before a clean kidney read. CK is not raised. The hair-loss link comes from one unreplicated small study.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.05 Test First; 05.09.01 Creatine; 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Creatine HCl, buffered creatine, creatine ethyl ester
entries.verdict_text: 'Fancier forms cost more and do not work better'
entries.why: They cost more and have no better results than monohydrate.
entries.source: 05.09.01 Creatine; 05.06.02 The Short List

entries.name: Liquid creatine
entries.why: It breaks down while it sits in the bottle.
entries.source: 05.09.01 Creatine

entries.name: Protein powder (general)
entries.verdict_text: Tier 1 — to hit your protein target
entries.why: A handy way to eat more protein, not a magic supplement. Use it if you can't hit ~0.8 g protein per lb of body weight from meals. If your food already hits your number, the powder adds very little. Cheap forms work as well as pricey ones for most people.
entries.dose_text: If a 3-day food log shows you are short by 20-60 g a day, take 1-2 scoops (most scoops hold 20-30 g protein). Target ~0.8 g/lb/day, 30-40 g per meal over 3-4 meals; after ~50, aim for 40 g+ per meal. Leucine threshold ~2.5-3 g per meal.
entries.forms: Whey (quick, leucine-rich), casein (slow, good at bedtime), egg, or plant blends (better with added leucine or a bit more). Buy a tested product (NSF Certified for Sport, Informed Sport, Informed Choice or Clean Label Project) with a full amino-acid profile and no proprietary blend. Plant and chocolate flavors carry the most heavy metals; rotate brands if you use a lot.
entries.timing: Total daily intake is the big deal. A post-training shake is handy, not required. 30-40 g of slow protein before bed can help overnight.
entries.interactions: With kidney disease, follow your specialist's protein limits. Allergens: whey and casein are dairy, soy is soy; with a dairy allergy, use egg or plant.
entries.side_effects: High protein and muscle can raise creatinine slightly (not kidney damage in a healthy lifter); very high intake can nudge uric acid. Watch for heavy metals and 'protein spiking' (free amino acids inflating the protein count).
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Whey protein (concentrate / isolate)
entries.verdict_text: 'Most people' — pick on taste, price and how your stomach feels
entries.why: Concentrate or isolate suits most people. It is fast and leucine-rich (DIAAS ~1.1), and in most cases whey beats EAAs.
entries.dose_text: ~25-30 g whey reaches the leucine threshold per meal.
entries.forms: Concentrate: ~70-80% protein with some lactose and fat; cheapest and creamiest. Isolate: ≥90% protein with very little lactose, for the dairy-sensitive.
entries.timing: Any time; useful after training.
entries.interactions: Dairy: avoid with a milk allergy.
entries.side_effects: Can upset the stomach if you are lactose intolerant; switch to isolate or plant.
entries.source: 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.09.06 EAAs, BCAAs, HMB and Glutamine; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Whey hydrolysate
entries.why: Pre-digested, fastest and most expensive, and it can taste bitter. It adds little real benefit over isolate.
entries.source: 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Casein protein
entries.why: Slow-digesting; gives amino acids for hours. Pick it before sleep or before a long gap between meals. Cottage cheese and Greek yogurt are casein-rich alternatives.
entries.dose_text: 30-40 g before bed.
entries.timing: Before bed or a long gap between meals.
entries.interactions: Avoid with a dairy allergy.
entries.source: 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Plant protein powders (pea, soy, rice, hemp, blends)
entries.verdict_text: 'Plant powders work' — use a blend (pea + rice) or soy/pea
entries.why: Plant isolates with added leucine, or larger doses, built muscle about as well as whey. Suited to vegans and dairy avoiders. Rice and hemp are weaker on their own (DIAAS: soy ~0.9, pea ~0.6-0.8).
entries.dose_text: 35-45 g per meal.
entries.forms: A pea + rice blend, or a soy or pea base; added leucine is a plus.
entries.side_effects: More lead, cadmium and arsenic than milk powders, so third-party testing matters more for daily use.
entries.source: 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Collagen (peptides / gelatin)
entries.verdict_text: 'Does not count toward your 0.8 grams per pound'
entries.why: Owner decision: not recommended. The vault says it does not count toward your muscle-building protein target (no tryptophan, little leucine, very low quality score). For other uses it is at best a modest add-on: tendon rehab 'a cheap add-on with some support', skin 'small gains are plausible', joints 'possible small help, low confidence'.
entries.dose_text: Studied doses if used: tendon/ligament ~15 g (10-20 g) gelatin or peptides + ~50 mg vitamin C, 30-60 min before loading; skin 2.5-10 g a day; joints ~10 g a day. A 15 g serving ≈ 60 kcal.
entries.forms: Hydrolyzed collagen peptides (mix hot or cold); gelatin works as well in studies; marine (skip with fish allergy); bovine (most common and cheapest); capsules are fine but you need many to reach 10 g. Beauty drinks and gummies usually hold 1-2 g, below the studied amount. Plant or vegan 'collagen' contains no collagen. Choose NSF Certified for Sport or USP Verified (hides and bones can hold heavy metals).
entries.timing: Tendon use: 30-60 minutes before training or rehab. Skin and joints: any time.
entries.cycling: Tendons: if you feel no difference in 2-3 months, stop spending. Joints: 2-3 months tracking weekly 0-10 pain. Skin: 8-12 weeks, then decide.
entries.interactions: Kidney stones: keep doses modest (hydroxyproline turns partly into oxalate). Cow or pig sources may conflict with religious or personal choices. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: stick to food amounts.
entries.side_effects: Very safe: fullness or mild stomach upset. Stop if you get a rash, swelling, hives or lasting stomach pain. It will not rebuild worn cartilage or heal a badly torn tendon.
entries.contradictions: Tendon dose: 05.14.03 gives about 15 g (10-20 g range); 05.14.04 gives 10-15 g.
entries.source: 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.14.03 Collagen; 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Plant / vegan 'collagen'
entries.why: Plant or vegan 'collagen' products contain no collagen.
entries.source: 05.14.03 Collagen

entries.name: Caffeine
entries.verdict_text: The best-proven performance aid; 'modestly helps endurance and power'
entries.why: The most used performance aid in the world, and the best proven. Gains in endurance, power, effort, attention and reaction time are real but modest. Coffee and tea do the job as well as a pill; plain tablets are cheap and let you control the dose. As a fat burner the effect is small, and tolerance builds within days to weeks.
entries.dose_text: Training 3-6 mg/kg (~1.4-2.7 mg/lb) ≈ 200-400 mg for most adults; start at 3 mg/kg. Alertness 50-200 mg. Under 400 mg a day from all sources; ~200 mg a day in pregnancy or for slow CYP1A2 clearers.
entries.timing: 30-60 minutes before training or a mental task. Half-life ~5-6 h: stop coffee 8-10 h before bed and pre-workouts ~13 h before bed. Train at night caffeine-free.
entries.cycling: Keep doses modest; cut back for a week if the effect fades; save bigger doses for hard sessions. Step down slowly (stopping abruptly causes headache, tiredness and low mood for a few days).
entries.interactions: Adds to stimulant medicines (ADHD meds), nicotine, synephrine and other fat-burner stimulants. Drugs cleared by the same liver enzyme can raise caffeine. Take extra care with high BP, irregular heartbeat, anxiety or pregnancy. Smoking speeds clearance; birth control and pregnancy slow it. Watch for stacking: coffee + pre-workout + energy drink + fat burner can reach 850 mg.
entries.side_effects: Racing heart, higher resting HR, jitters, anxiety, poor light sleep, stomach upset, creeping BP. 400 mg six hours before bed cut sleep by ~1 h. Chest pain, fainting, or a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle means stop and get checked.
entries.source: 05.09.03 Caffeine and Pre-Workouts; 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.10.03 L-Theanine; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Pre-workout products
entries.verdict_text: 'Most pre-workouts are caffeine plus a little theater'
entries.why: You do not need a pre-workout to train hard. Proprietary blends hide doses, citrulline and beta-alanine are often underdosed, the creatine scoop is too small, 'focus' extracts have thin evidence, and aggressive ones may hold other stimulants under odd names. Cheaper plan: caffeine 30-60 min before, creatine 3-5 g daily, optional citrulline 6-8 g, beta-alanine if your efforts last 1-4 minutes.
entries.timing: If caffeinated, ~13 h before bed.
entries.interactions: Avoid in pregnancy and for teens. Tested athletes: NSF Certified for Sport or Informed Sport only. Count the caffeine.
entries.side_effects: Racing heart, bad sleep, BP rise; hidden stimulants.
entries.source: 05.09.03 Caffeine and Pre-Workouts; 05.06.03 Buying Supplements; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: L-theanine (incl. caffeine + L-theanine)
entries.verdict_text: 'Calms without sedating'; with caffeine the 'best-proven mix'
entries.why: One of the safest supplements you can buy: a small, safe nudge toward calm. It is the first pick for a racing mind at bedtime and for jittery coffee drinkers. With caffeine (2:1), it improved attention and reaction time more than caffeine alone, with fewer side effects. Effects are modest, and it does not treat an anxiety disorder.
entries.dose_text: Sleep: 200 mg 30-60 min before bed (research range 100-400 mg/day). Daytime calm: 100-200 mg as needed. Stress studies: 200-400 mg a day. With caffeine: ~200 mg theanine + 100 mg caffeine (some use 1:1).
entries.forms: Pure L form (e.g. Suntheanine), third-party tested. Avoid racemic D/L mixes and 'calm' or 'sleep' blends hiding the dose. Magnesium-theanine combos are fine if each dose is listed.
entries.timing: 30-60 minutes before bed; with or just before coffee or tea. Reaches the brain in ~30 min.
entries.cycling: No need to cycle or taper; no dependence, tolerance or withdrawal. Trial 1-2 weeks and stop if nothing changes.
entries.interactions: Adds to blood-pressure medicine and sedatives. Pregnancy: tea amounts are fine; at supplement doses, lean toward caution. If you still feel wired, remove the stimulant instead of adding more. It does not prevent caffeine dependence.
entries.side_effects: Rare mild headache or upset stomach. Safe for older adults at standard doses.
entries.source: 05.10.03 L-Theanine; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.09.03 Caffeine and Pre-Workouts; 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Beta-alanine
entries.why: A fair pick only if you do hard 1-4 minute efforts (400-1,500 m runs, 100-400 m swims, combat rounds, circuits), have the basics in place, and will stick with it for 8-12+ weeks; expect ~2-3%. If you lift for strength, jog easy or train for health, skip it. It is not a strength or muscle builder.
entries.dose_text: 3.2-6.4 g a day, every day, in 0.8-1.6 g servings a few hours apart (3-4 servings); start near the low end.
entries.forms: Single ingredient with a stated dose; sustained-release cuts the tingle. Underdosed pre-workouts (often well under 3.2 g) will not load your muscles.
entries.timing: Timing doesn't matter (no pre-workout boost); e.g. breakfast, lunch and dinner.
entries.cycling: Daily for ≥8-12 weeks; keep taking it to hold the benefit. Test a hard sport-specific effort before and after.
entries.interactions: No serious drug interactions known. It shares a transporter with taurine (theoretical at very large doses). Pairs with creatine; a small extra gain with sodium bicarbonate.
entries.side_effects: Harmless tingling (paresthesia) 10-20 min after a dose, fading within ~1 h; it is dose-dependent and not a sign that it works.
entries.source: 05.09.04 Beta-Alanine; 05.09.03 Caffeine and Pre-Workouts; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Carnosine pills
entries.why: Most is broken down before it reaches muscle; do not buy carnosine pills in place of beta-alanine.
entries.source: 05.09.04 Beta-Alanine; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: L-citrulline / citrulline malate
entries.verdict_text: 'The better of the pump supplements'; best case (with Korean red ginseng) on the libido list
entries.why: Gym benefits are modest: less soreness is the steadiest finding, plus a fuller pump; reps are mixed, and it is not shown to build strength or muscle. Daily ≥~6 g gives a small BP drop. For erections the evidence is thin (one small study in mild ED); effects are small, but it is one worth a trial.
entries.dose_text: L-citrulline ~6-8 g; citrulline malate (2:1) ~8 g (≈5 g citrulline). 6 g of malate at 2:1 is only ~4 g citrulline, under the studied dose. No firm dose for sex.
entries.forms: Pure L-citrulline (better for BP goals or stacking) or citrulline malate 2:1 (most studied for exercise; the ratio must be stated). Avoid proprietary 'NO blends'.
entries.timing: ~60 minutes before training.
entries.cycling: Gym: full dose for 2-3 weeks; if you see nothing, stop. Libido: test for 2-3 months.
entries.interactions: With BP medicines, PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) or nitrates (nitroglycerin), pressure can drop too low; check with a pharmacist. Avoid loading around planned surgery.
entries.side_effects: Well tolerated; far less stomach trouble than arginine. Fainting or chest pain means get help fast.
entries.source: 05.09.05 Citrulline, Arginine and Beetroot; 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: L-arginine (incl. arginine AKG, 'NO blends')
entries.verdict_text: 'Weak when taken by mouth' — 'Citrulline is the better choice'
entries.why: Arginase in the gut and liver breaks it down on first pass, so citrulline raises blood arginine more. Fancy versions (arginine AKG, exotic NO compounds) are not backed by research.
entries.dose_text: 3-6 g if trying; daily ≥~6 g may lower BP a little.
entries.interactions: Same BP/PDE5/nitrate cautions as citrulline; avoid loading around surgery. Skip it if you are prone to cold sores (herpes).
entries.side_effects: Cramps, gas and loose stools at higher doses; can trigger cold sores.
entries.source: 05.09.05 Citrulline, Arginine and Beetroot; 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Beetroot juice / dietary nitrate
entries.why: The strongest case of anything in its chapter for endurance (running, cycling, swimming, rowing): small but real gains, best for recreational or moderately trained athletes and smaller in the highly trained. No benefit shown for heavy lifting. Small BP drop.
entries.dose_text: ~6-12 mmol nitrate (~370-740 mg); little added benefit beyond ~12 mmol.
entries.forms: One or two concentrated beetroot 'shots' with nitrate stated in mmol or mg. Avoid products that only say 'beetroot extract'; many powders carry very little.
entries.timing: ~2-3 h before the event (nitrite peak). Skip antibacterial mouthwash and tongue scraping around the dose; they cancel the benefit.
entries.cycling: 3+ days in a row may build a bigger effect.
entries.interactions: Same BP-medicine, PDE5-inhibitor and nitroglycerin cautions as citrulline. With a history of oxalate kidney stones, keep beet products moderate. Surgery caution.
entries.side_effects: Beeturia (red or pink urine or stool) is harmless. No blood test measures nitric oxide.
entries.source: 05.09.05 Citrulline, Arginine and Beetroot; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Essential amino acids (EAAs)
entries.verdict_text: 'Can help' for low-protein meals, fasted lifting, older age
entries.why: A much better pick than BCAAs, but they still don't beat real protein most of the time; in most cases whey wins. Useful for a low-protein meal, fasted training, older adults, plant-based eaters or poor appetite.
entries.dose_text: ~10 g per serving with ≥2.5 g leucine.
entries.forms: All nine EAAs listed with exact grams; no proprietary blend; third-party seal if tested.
entries.interactions: ~4 kcal/g; it turns on muscle building, so it breaks a fast.
entries.side_effects: Well tolerated.
entries.source: 05.09.06 EAAs, BCAAs, HMB and Glutamine; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: BCAAs (branched-chain amino acids)
entries.why: Only 3 of the 9 EAAs, so muscle building stalls; they add almost nothing if you eat ~0.8 g/lb protein. 'Better than nothing' only as a last-resort quick option. Beware hidden 'amino blend' amounts.
entries.side_effects: Generally safe.
entries.source: 05.09.06 EAAs, BCAAs, HMB and Glutamine; 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: HMB (beta-hydroxy beta-methylbutyrate)
entries.why: A small bet for beginners or people returning to training (first couple of months) and for older adults holding muscle through illness, bed rest or injury. Experienced lifters with enough protein should skip it and spend the money on food.
entries.dose_text: ~3 g a day, often 3 × 1 g with meals.
entries.forms: Calcium HMB is most studied; free-acid HMB may absorb faster but has less long-term study.
entries.timing: Daily, a bit before exercise in studies; consistency matters more than exact time.
entries.cycling: Judge after ≥3-4 weeks.
entries.side_effects: Well tolerated for weeks to months; long-term data limited. Not banned.
entries.source: 05.09.06 EAAs, BCAAs, HMB and Glutamine; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Glutamine
entries.why: Reviews show no effect on body composition, muscle gain or immune function in healthy, well-fed people, so a healthy lifter should skip it. Narrow exception: for post-infectious IBS with diarrhea, a trial is 'reasonable, with modest hopes'. For gut-barrier use it is early-stage and overhyped.
entries.dose_text: Gut symptoms or hard diet: 5-10 g a day. Post-infectious IBS-D: ~5 g three times a day for ~4 weeks.
entries.forms: Plain glutamine with the dose on the label; beware token-dose 'recovery blends'.
entries.interactions: Be careful with significant liver disease (ammonia). Avoid megadosing.
entries.side_effects: Generally well tolerated. In very sick patients, high doses harmed some.
entries.source: 05.09.06 EAAs, BCAAs, HMB and Glutamine; 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Leucine (plain)
entries.verdict_text: Does not build muscle if the meal is short on protein
entries.why: Extra leucine alone does not build muscle when total protein is low. It has a possible small role for older adults or plant eaters with a slightly low-protein meal, but adding more food protein works as well.
entries.dose_text: Sold in 3-5 g servings.
entries.source: 05.09.06 EAAs, BCAAs, HMB and Glutamine; 05.09.02 Protein Powder; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda)
entries.verdict_text: Ranked best of the six performance aids — for 1-10 minute hard efforts, if your stomach can take it
entries.why: Real research backs it for ~1-10 minute hard efforts (400-1,500 m, rowing races, repeated hard intervals): gains from a small slice of a percent to a few percent. It rarely matters in a normal gym session and does little for max strength or long steady endurance.
entries.forms: Powder, or gel/coated capsules that release later with fewer GI issues.
entries.timing: 60-180 min before, split over 30-60 min, with a small carb meal and water. Never try it for the first time on race day.
test_first: CO2 on blood panel (with large frequent use)
entries.interactions: Avoid with high blood pressure, heart failure, kidney disease or a low-sodium diet (each dose carries several grams of sodium). Small extra gain with beta-alanine. Legal in sport.
entries.side_effects: Bloating, gas, cramps, nausea, loose stools.
entries.source: 05.09.07 Sodium Bicarbonate, Carnitine and Other Performance Aids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: L-carnitine / L-carnitine L-tartrate (LCLT)
entries.verdict_text: 'Does not reliably burn more fat'; 'helps only when truly low'
entries.why: For most people the trade does not look worth it: a small recovery gain offset by the TMAO question. It does not reliably help healthy people burn more fat, so it is not worth the money for fat loss. A true shortage (e.g. some dialysis patients) is treated as medicine.
entries.dose_text: If trying for recovery: LCLT 1-2 g a day for 4 weeks. Oral doses in studies: ~1-3 g a day.
entries.interactions: Can raise INR on warfarin. Skip it with heart disease, kidney disease, a high TMAO result, seizures or warfarin. On thyroid medicine, check with a pharmacist.
entries.side_effects: Nausea, stomach cramps, loose stools, fishy body odor. Raises TMAO in many people (linked to clogged arteries and heart events, still debated). More seizures in people who already have them.
entries.source: 05.09.07 Sodium Bicarbonate, Carnitine and Other Performance Aids; 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Tart cherry (Montmorency)
entries.verdict_text: Ranked 2nd; 'use it in hard weeks, not all year'
entries.why: Modest help with soreness and strength return during hard weeks (races, tournaments, heavy blocks); clearer in trained athletes. Not an everyday must-have. Sleep claims are thin and inconsistent. It is linked to fewer gout flares and slightly lower uric acid.
entries.dose_text: ~30 mL concentrate or ~8 oz juice, twice a day (05.13.07: ~8-12 oz juice twice a day or the equivalent).
entries.forms: Pure Montmorency juice, concentrate or powder, with no added sugar and a clear amount per serving.
entries.timing: Start 4-5 days before a hard event and continue 2-3 days after.
entries.cycling: Hard weeks only; skip it in easy training.
