entries.side_effects: Large amounts can loosen stools (sorbitol). Juice adds sugar and calories.
entries.contradictions: Juice amount: 05.09.07 gives ~8 oz twice a day; 05.13.07 gives ~8-12 oz twice a day.
entries.source: 05.09.07 Sodium Bicarbonate, Carnitine and Other Performance Aids; 05.13.07 Curcumin, Boswellia and Other Anti-Inflammatories; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Taurine
entries.why: A small gain for endurance and a small blood-pressure effect (its best-supported use is prehypertension or high BP). Cheap and safe. Longevity claims are unproven, and it does not reliably calm caffeine jitters (in energy drinks, the caffeine does the work).
entries.dose_text: Common 1-3 g a day; for heart goals ~1.5-3 g every day; for exercise a single 1-2 g dose. Studies went up to ~6 g at once with no clear dose-response between 1 and 6 g.
entries.forms: Plain taurine powder with the dose stated; synthetic is fine; a fermentation-made vegan option exists.
entries.timing: Exercise: 1-2 h before training. Heart: timing not critical.
entries.interactions: Can lower BP further with BP medicine; with heart disease on medicine, do not add it on your own. Shares a transporter with beta-alanine.
entries.side_effects: Well tolerated up to several grams a day.
entries.source: 05.09.07 Sodium Bicarbonate, Carnitine and Other Performance Aids; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.09.04 Beta-Alanine; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Glycerol (hyperhydration)
entries.why: Skip it for training. It may help only in a long hot race with no good chance to drink, and endurance gains in heat are small and inconsistent.
entries.dose_text: ~1 g/kg with 20-25 mL fluid/kg, 1-2 h before the event.
entries.interactions: Removed from the banned list in 2018; check the current list.
entries.side_effects: Headache, nausea, bloating, dizziness, water weight. A big plain-water intake can dilute blood sodium to unsafe levels.
entries.source: 05.09.07 Sodium Bicarbonate, Carnitine and Other Performance Aids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Ketone drinks (esters / salts)
entries.verdict_text: 'Mixed results, often upset the stomach, not a fat burner'
entries.why: Ranked weakest (6th) of the performance aids. For most people they are a waste of effort; some studies found worse performance. Esters raise blood ketones more than salts, taste bitter and are very expensive.
entries.interactions: Avoid with type 1 diabetes or diabetes medicine (ketoacidosis confusion).
entries.side_effects: Nausea, loose stools.
entries.source: 05.09.07 Sodium Bicarbonate, Carnitine and Other Performance Aids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Turkesterone (Ajuga turkestanica)
entries.why: There is no real human proof for muscle. Independent tests found many products hold less than the label, some almost none. If you try it anyway, treat it as an experiment (one product, 8-10 weeks, a countable measure) and expect little.
entries.forms: If tried: mg of turkesterone per serving (not 'extract'), standardization %, batch COA, NSF Certified for Sport or Informed Sport, no proprietary blend.
entries.side_effects: Long-term human data is thin; the main risk is spiking with real drugs.
entries.source: 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Ecdysterone (beta-ecdysterone)
entries.why: One small 10-week trial in young resistance-trained men used pure measured ecdysterone and has not been repeated. Little survives the gut (animal data). It is of interest to anti-doping, so if you are drug tested, check current rules.
entries.source: 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Epicatechin (as an anabolic pill)
entries.why: Very small, short studies on myostatin/follistatin markers; muscle changes small or unclear. Cocoa and dark chocolate as food are fine.
entries.source: 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Laxogenin (5-alpha-hydroxy laxogenin)
entries.why: Almost no good human research; promoted as 'a steroid without the side effects'. It is a lab-altered compound with a poor label-matching record.
entries.source: 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Prohormones / 'legal steroids'
entries.why: Old prohormones were real steroid drugs; some were later controlled by law because of serious harm. A product can sit on a store shelf and still be a steroid.
entries.source: 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: SARMs / 'research chemicals'
entries.verdict_text: Avoid — stay away from anything that promises steroid-level results
entries.why: Experimental and not approved; the FDA warns against SARMs in bodybuilding products. A 2017 analysis of 44 products found ~half held a SARM, ~1 in 4 had unlisted substances and ~59% had wrong amounts. 'Not for human consumption' is a legal dodge. Risks: testosterone suppression, cholesterol changes, liver stress, failed drug tests.
entries.side_effects: Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, severe itching (liver); chest pain, shortness of breath, or one swollen painful leg (clot): get care fast.
entries.source: 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Melatonin
entries.verdict_text: 'A chronobiotic … not a hypnotic'; ranked best of the sleep stack
entries.why: A real tool for body-clock problems (jet lag, shift work, delayed sleep phase, older age), but only a modest help for falling asleep: it shortens sleep onset by ~7-12 min. It is not a cure for insomnia, stress, apnea or bad habits. Labels are often wrong (83% below to 478% above the label in one study).
entries.dose_text: 0.3-0.5 mg to shift the clock (matches natural production); 1-4 mg for sleep itself, with benefit peaking at ~4 mg a day. Stay at or under 4 mg; 10 mg and up is 'research territory', and 40-60 mg is never a sleep dose. Start at 0.5-1 mg and use the lowest dose that works. Jet lag east: 0.5-3 mg.
entries.forms: Immediate-release is best for falling asleep or shifting the clock. Prolonged-release is aimed at staying asleep and is better studied in older adults. Avoid 5 or 10 mg gummies ('the wrong tool') and sleep blends. Pick single-ingredient, USP Verified.
entries.timing: For sleep: 1-4 mg about 3 hours before your target sleep time (not 2 mg 30 min before bed). Late clock: ~0.5 mg in the early evening plus bright light after waking. East travel: evening by destination time plus morning light. Night shift: optional low dose before the daytime sleep block.
entries.cycling: Trial 1-2 weeks with a morning note. Long-term data are limited; if you need it nightly for months and still sleep badly, look at light, schedule and CBT-I.
entries.interactions: Check with a pharmacist if you take blood thinners, immune-calming drugs, BP or diabetes medicines, or sedatives (adds to alcohol and sedatives). Hold off if pregnant, with untreated sleep apnea, or when stress, caffeine, alcohol or a bright bedroom is the real problem. Children: keep gummies out of reach and see a pediatrician. A big lingering dose can nudge morning fasting glucose up.
entries.side_effects: Morning grogginess, vivid dreams, headache; most come from too much or from taking it too late.
entries.source: 05.10.01 Melatonin; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.06.03 Buying Supplements; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Glycine
entries.verdict_text: 'Cheap and safe, with a modest sleep benefit; worth considering.'
entries.why: One of the better-backed and safest sleep helpers ('modest but real'): it lowers core body temperature and reduces next-day sleepiness after short nights. Not shown to fix serious insomnia. It also supports collagen and connective tissue alongside collagen peptides.
entries.dose_text: ~3 g (3,000 mg) before bed (range 3-5 g); collagen support 3-5 g a day.
entries.forms: Plain powder in water or tea (mildly sweet; too large a dose for capsules). Single ingredient, third-party tested.
entries.timing: 30-60 minutes before bed.
entries.cycling: A one-to-two-week experiment; judge by sleep onset and next-day feel.
entries.interactions: Avoid mixing with alcohol or prescription sleeping pills; check with a pharmacist on sleep or psychiatric medicine. Don't take before driving. Pairs with evening magnesium.
entries.side_effects: Very safe; high doses cause mild stomach upset or sleepiness. Loud snoring, gasping or heavy daytime sleepiness need sleep-apnea testing, not a powder.
entries.source: 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Apigenin
entries.why: The biggest reputation and the thinnest proof: lab GABA-A binding only, with very little human sleep research. Treat it as optional; ranked last in the sleep stack.
entries.dose_text: Commonly 50 mg before bed; this comes from popular use, not a sleep trial.
entries.timing: Before bed.
entries.interactions: Do not mix with alcohol, prescription sleep drugs or other sedatives.
entries.side_effects: Long-term pill safety data is thin.
entries.source: 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Chamomile (tea)
entries.why: A cup in the evening costs little and gives you a calming ritual, but there is little controlled evidence: a low-risk experiment, not a reliable tool.
entries.dose_text: A cup in the evening.
entries.source: 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD

entries.name: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera)
entries.verdict_text: 'Strongest adaptogen research'; stress 'Best support', sleep 'Modest help', testosterone 'Small and mixed', strength 'Weak'
entries.why: For a stressed person with no thyroid, liver or autoimmune issues, a 600 mg extract for 8-12 weeks has a reasonable record (cortisol down ~1.16 mcg/dL). In stressed, tired or overweight men, testosterone rose ~10-15% over placebo; a calm, well-rested man should not expect that. For others, the risks may outweigh the gain.
entries.dose_text: 300-600 mg a day of standardized root extract; most positive studies used 600 mg a day for 8-12 weeks. Start with 300 mg a day in week 1, then 600 mg if tolerated.
entries.forms: A branded, clinically studied standardized extract: KSM-66 (root only, ~5% withanolides) or Sensoril (root + leaf, more sedating). Avoid plain root powder, unlabeled 'ashwagandha' and 'adrenal' or 'stress' blends. Look for a third-party seal.
entries.timing: All at once or split into two; in the evening if sleep is a goal; with food if your stomach is upset.
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks on, then a break (no taper needed). Decide at 8-12 weeks and stop if nothing changed.
entries.interactions: Skip with pregnancy or trying to conceive, breastfeeding, liver disease, hyperthyroid, autoimmune thyroid, thyroid medicine, or autoimmune disease (unless cleared). It may raise thyroid hormone, adds to sedatives and alcohol, may add to blood-sugar and BP drugs, and may work against immunosuppressants. Stop a couple of weeks before surgery.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset, drowsiness. Rare liver injury: stop and get checked for dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, itching, upper-right belly pain. Thyroid stimulation (racing heart, sweating, weight loss, shaky hands): stop and test. Emotional blunting reported.
entries.source: 05.10.04 Ashwagandha; 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Rhodiola rosea
entries.why: Possibly helpful, not proven, mostly for mental or physical tiredness under stress. It is not a proven way to run faster or lift more.
entries.dose_text: 200-600 mg a day (standardized to ~3% rosavins and 1% salidroside).
entries.forms: A standardized extract (e.g. clinically studied SHR-5). Choose a DNA-verified species with third-party testing; fakes use cheaper species or lab-made rosavins.
entries.timing: Morning or before a stressful task; a late dose can wreck your sleep.
entries.cycling: On and off or in short blocks, not nonstop (adaptogen cycles ~8-12 weeks; a clean trial is 4-8 weeks).
entries.interactions: Clashes with antidepressants and stimulants; caution in bipolar; may add to blood-sugar and BP medicine.
entries.side_effects: Jitters, trouble sleeping, vivid dreams.
entries.source: 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Panax ginseng (Asian / Korean red ginseng)
entries.why: The evidence is modest: a small possible lift in tiredness in some people, with mixed exercise results. For erections, Korean red ginseng gave a modest gain in erection scores in men with mild to moderate trouble (low-to-moderate quality trials); evidence in women is thin.
entries.dose_text: Adaptogen use: ~200-400 mg a day of standardized extract (go by the label, not raw root weight). Libido: ~2,000-3,000 mg a day of red ginseng, split into a few doses.
entries.forms: Standardized extract naming the species and listing ginsenoside %; Korean red ginseng is steamed, dried root. Third-party tested; avoid proprietary blends with a tiny pinch.
entries.timing: Morning or midday (it can keep you awake); libido dose split through the day.
entries.cycling: Cycles of a few weeks to a few months. Libido: ~2-3 months; if it hasn't helped within three months, stop.
entries.interactions: Lowers blood sugar (diabetes medicine); BP up or down; may weaken warfarin; may not mix with MAOIs, stimulants or some antidepressants. Stop about two weeks before surgery.
entries.side_effects: Trouble sleeping, jitters, headache, stomach upset.
entries.contradictions: Two different doses for two uses: ~200-400 mg/day extract (05.10.05) vs ~2,000-3,000 mg/day red ginseng for erections (05.11.07).
entries.source: 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius)
entries.why: Milder and calmer than Asian ginseng; the evidence is modest. Small trials found fewer or shorter colds and lower post-meal blood sugar.
entries.dose_text: Not separately stated; go by a standardized label.
entries.interactions: Same cautions as Panax ginseng: blood sugar, warfarin, MAOIs and stimulants; stop before surgery.
entries.source: 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Cordyceps
entries.why: Exercise data is weak, mixed and from small, poorly made studies. Many farm-grown products are mostly grain starch with little cordycepin.
entries.dose_text: Studied ~1-3 g a day of whole product.
entries.forms: If tried: label must state the species and active compounds; look for 'fruiting body'.
entries.source: 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Holy basil (tulsi)
entries.why: May lower stress and improve mood a little, but trial quality is low and it does not beat ashwagandha.
entries.dose_text: 300-600 mg a day of extract.
entries.interactions: May lower blood sugar (diabetes medicine) and may thin the blood a little (blood thinners; stop before surgery). Avoid in pregnancy and when trying to conceive (animal data suggests lower fertility).
entries.source: 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Eleuthero (Siberian ginseng)
entries.why: Most studies show little effect. Trying it for a flat or low-cortisol pattern is a guess, not a proven use.
entries.dose_text: 300-1,200 mg a day of extract.
entries.interactions: Plant mix-ups are reported, so use third-party testing. Caution with high blood pressure and blood thinners.
entries.side_effects: Mild: stomach upset, trouble sleeping, headache.
entries.source: 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 'Adrenal' / 'stress' adaptogen blends
entries.why: Proprietary blends hide doses, and 'adrenal fatigue' is not a real medical condition. 'Fix your adrenals' claims are a red flag.
entries.source: 05.10.05 Rhodiola, Ginseng, Cordyceps and Other Adaptogens; 05.10.04 Ashwagandha

entries.name: Saffron extract (Crocus sativus)
entries.why: Good evidence and the fewest problems for mild to moderate low mood: ~30 mg a day beat placebo and matched SSRIs in reviews (small trials, many from Iran). For sleep with stress or low mood it is a credible option, not a miracle. For a healthy adult on no antidepressants, 28 mg a day is a low-risk trial.
entries.dose_text: Mood: 28-30 mg a day (often 14 mg morning + 14 mg night). Sleep: 14-28 mg. Above ~1.5 g a day trouble begins; ~5 g causes bleeding; ~20 g is potentially deadly.
entries.forms: A studied standardized extract stating crocins/safranal (e.g. '3.5% Lepticrosalides'); affron has the most rigorous trials. Avoid plain kitchen saffron and cheap generic capsules ('a coin flip', often faked) or blends.
entries.timing: Mood: split 14 mg morning and 14 mg night, or one evening dose for mood plus sleep. Sleep: about 1 hour before bed.
entries.cycling: Wait 1-4 weeks to judge.
entries.interactions: Avoid in pregnancy at any dose. Bipolar: only with a clinician. Do not combine with SSRIs or SNRIs without medical guidance. Check blood thinners and BP or diabetes meds with a pharmacist. Low mood for >2 weeks needs real care; self-harm thoughts are an emergency.
entries.side_effects: Very well tolerated at 28-30 mg a day.
entries.source: 05.10.06 Saffron, 5-HTP, SAM-e and St. John's Wort; 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan)
entries.why: The thinnest data (few small, older, poor-quality trials), and it can cause dangerous serotonin syndrome with antidepressants. Not a first pick.
entries.dose_text: Mostly 50-300 mg a day, starting low to reduce nausea; trouble above ~1.5 g.
entries.forms: Third-party tested brand only (contamination history).
entries.interactions: Do not combine with antidepressants, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol or dextromethorphan (serotonin syndrome: agitation, sweating, shaking, fast heartbeat, fever, twitching; this is an emergency). It needs B6 to convert, but do not megadose B6.
entries.side_effects: Nausea, stomach upset, diarrhea, drowsiness.
entries.source: 05.10.06 Saffron, 5-HTP, SAM-e and St. John's Wort; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: SAM-e (S-adenosylmethionine)
entries.verdict_text: 'Some data, mostly from small or older trials'
entries.why: Some benefit, mainly when added to an antidepressant, but reviews are mixed and low quality. Not a first pick.
entries.dose_text: About 400-1,600 mg a day.
entries.forms: Enteric-coated tablets in sealed blister packs (it breaks down fast in air).
entries.interactions: Can trigger mania in bipolar; may add to antidepressants and cause serotonin syndrome.
entries.side_effects: Nausea, gut upset, anxiety, trouble sleeping.
entries.source: 05.10.06 Saffron, 5-HTP, SAM-e and St. John's Wort; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum)
entries.verdict_text: 'Most studied, but it clashes with a long list of medicines'
entries.why: A real option for mild to moderate depression (not shown to work for severe depression), with a long list of drug interactions.
entries.dose_text: 900-1,200 mg a day, often split into 3 doses.
entries.forms: Extract standardized to 0.3% hypericin.
entries.cycling: 4-6 weeks to judge.
entries.interactions: An enzyme inducer (speeds CYP3A4): it weakens birth control, warfarin, some HIV, transplant, cancer and heart drugs, statins and many others, and the effect lasts ~2 weeks after stopping. Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans and tramadol. Avoid in bipolar and pregnancy. Do not stop a prescribed antidepressant to switch. Flag before surgery.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset, dry mouth, dizziness, sun sensitivity.
entries.source: 05.10.06 Saffron, 5-HTP, SAM-e and St. John's Wort; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: GABA pills
entries.why: The evidence is thin and the basic science has a hole in it: GABA is thought to cross the blood-brain barrier poorly. L-theanine, magnesium and glycine are a better use of your money.
entries.dose_text: Labels ~100-750 mg; studies often 100-300 mg.
entries.cycling: If you feel nothing in two weeks, stop.
entries.interactions: Not with alcohol or sedating medicines.
entries.side_effects: Usually mild: tingling, flushing, warm face, drowsiness.
entries.source: 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Phenibut
entries.why: Tolerance builds fast, and stopping after regular use causes severe withdrawal (anxiety, insomnia, sometimes seizures). The FDA says it is not a legal dietary ingredient, and some countries ban it. Stay away from it.
entries.source: 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Valerian root
entries.why: Reviews are mixed to null. If you try it, treat it as an experiment.
entries.dose_text: 300-600 mg extract; tea 2-3 g dried root.
entries.timing: 30 minutes to 2 hours before bed; may need 2-4 weeks of nightly use.
entries.interactions: Adds to alcohol, sleeping pills and anti-anxiety meds. Stop ~two weeks before surgery. Avoid in pregnancy.
entries.side_effects: Headache, stomach upset, dizziness, morning grogginess, vivid dreams; rare liver injury (mostly mixed products).
entries.source: 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Kava (kavalactones)
entries.verdict_text: 'Most evidence of benefit … Also the most serious risk, to the liver'
entries.why: Has the most evidence for short-term anxiety, though a later larger GAD trial found no benefit over placebo. It is less proven for sleep and carries a real risk of liver injury.
entries.dose_text: About 120-250 mg kavalactones a day.
entries.forms: Label must state kavalactones, from root (leaves and stems are a possible liver-risk factor). Traditional water-based drinks may be safer (not proven).
entries.cycling: Trials ran 4-24 weeks; the studied range is weeks to a few months.
entries.interactions: Never combine with alcohol. Avoid with liver disease, liver-straining drugs (e.g. frequent acetaminophen), sedating or anti-anxiety medicine, pregnancy or breastfeeding. No driving until you know your reaction. Flag before surgery.
entries.side_effects: Drowsiness; rare serious liver injury (some needed transplants). Stop and get care for yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, upper-right belly pain, unusual tiredness or nausea.
entries.source: 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: CBD (cannabidiol)
entries.verdict_text: Proven only as a prescription for rare seizures; anxiety and sleep 'small and mixed'
entries.why: Treat CBD as an experiment with uncertain odds. Anxiety evidence is mixed and sleep evidence is weak, and labels are unreliable.
entries.dose_text: No agreed dose; anxiety studies used ~25-300 mg a day. Start at 10-25 mg and go up slowly.
entries.forms: Get a recent independent certificate of analysis (CBD, THC, heavy metals); a sport seal such as Informed Sport for tested athletes. Full-spectrum contains trace THC.
entries.interactions: Slows liver enzymes and raises levels of warfarin and some seizure meds; higher doses can raise liver enzymes. Can cause a positive THC drug test even if 'THC-free'. Avoid in pregnancy or breastfeeding; check local laws.
entries.side_effects: Sleepiness, diarrhea, appetite changes.
entries.source: 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Sleep / 'calm' blends
entries.why: They often hide doses and contain too little of each ingredient. Pick single ingredients at a listed dose instead.
entries.source: 05.10.01 Melatonin; 05.10.03 L-Theanine

entries.name: 'PM' sleep pills (diphenhydramine, doxylamine)
entries.why: A poor long-term tool. Tolerance builds within days, they cause next-day grogginess and block acetylcholine, and heavy long-term use is linked to higher dementia risk, especially in older adults.
entries.source: 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Prescription sleep drugs (benzodiazepines, z-drugs) as a long-term fix
entries.verdict_text: Not a substitute for fixing habits and CBT-I
entries.why: They can work short term but carry tolerance, rebound insomnia and next-day effects. They are prescription drugs, not supplements.
entries.source: 05.10.02 The Sleep Stack - Magnesium, Glycine and Apigenin; 05.10.07 GABA, Valerian, Kava and CBD

entries.name: Testosterone boosters (general / proprietary blends)
entries.verdict_text: 'If your levels are normal, expect nothing.'
entries.why: Most boosters are useless, not dangerous: they do not raise testosterone in a man who already has normal levels. The real danger is the hidden drug (anabolic steroids, SARMs, stimulants), which brings failed drug tests and unexplained liver injury. Skip them entirely if you are trying for children soon, are drug tested, are a woman, or take unchecked prescriptions.
entries.interactions: Check prescriptions with a pharmacist. Fix shortages (vitamin D, zinc, magnesium) and lifestyle first. Avoid in pregnancy and for teens. Do not start three things at once.
entries.side_effects: Adulteration with steroids, SARMs or stimulants; liver injury.
entries.source: 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.11.03 Fadogia, Tribulus and Fenugreek; 05.11.04 Shilajit, Maca and Other Herbal Boosters; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia)
entries.verdict_text: 'A modest signal, but the studies are small'
entries.why: A reasonable herb to try, but the evidence is not yet convincing. It may help older, stressed or low-T men a little (most consistent in men over ~40 with low or low-normal T) and does little for healthy young men.
entries.dose_text: 200-400 mg a day of a standardized water extract; start at the low end; do not take more because 'more must work better'.
entries.forms: Standardized water extract (what the trials used), labelled 'extract' with a ratio (e.g. 100:1) and a marker (eurycomanone or glycosaponins); a clinically studied branded extract; third-party tested; single ingredient. Avoid plain root powder and 'T-matrix' blends.
entries.timing: With a meal in the morning or at midday; keep away from evening (restlessness, sleep).
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks, then retest and decide. There is no good evidence that cycling matters ('5 on/2 off' etc.). If it did nothing, stop.
entries.interactions: Check prescriptions with a pharmacist (BP, blood-sugar, hormone medicines, blood thinners). Avoid with pregnancy or breastfeeding, hormone-sensitive cancer, trying for a child soon, or as a drug-tested athlete without a sport seal. Not a sensible place to start for women.
entries.side_effects: Trouble sleeping, restlessness or irritability, upset stomach; long-term safety data is limited. Fakes, lead and mercury, and hidden sildenafil are quality risks. Yellow skin, dark urine, belly pain, racing heartbeat, chest pain or fainting: stop and get help.
entries.source: 05.11.02 Tongkat Ali; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.11.03 Fadogia, Tribulus and Fenugreek; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Fadogia agrestis
entries.why: Do not take fadogia to raise testosterone: the benefit is unproven and the risk is real. In rats it caused dose-dependent harm to the testes, liver and kidneys, and no safe dose is known. 'Nothing worth the risk. Skip it.'
entries.interactions: If you are trying to have children, do not use it at all. It is often hidden in blends with tongkat ali.
entries.side_effects: Unverified reports: nausea, stomach pain, headaches, flat mood. Liver or kidney harm can be silent until advanced. Yellow skin, dark urine, belly pain or much less urine: get care fast.
entries.source: 05.11.03 Fadogia, Tribulus and Fenugreek; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Tribulus terrestris
entries.verdict_text: 'Has shown no useful change in testosterone'; 'skip'
entries.why: Tribulus does not raise testosterone in healthy men; most studies show no change in androgens. At most it is a gentle try for libido with realistic hopes (thin evidence, maybe placebo), with no clear gain for lifters.
entries.dose_text: Not fixed; varies a lot between studies and products (often standardized to saponins).
entries.interactions: Avoid if pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset, trouble sleeping; rare reports of liver or kidney problems with impure products.
entries.source: 05.11.03 Fadogia, Tribulus and Fenugreek; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: D-aspartic acid (DAA)
entries.why: Early boosts did not hold up in lifters, and 6 g a day lowered testosterone. It has failed in trained men.
entries.source: 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.09.08 Turkesterone, Ecdysterone and 'Natural Anabolics'; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Fenugreek
entries.why: For testosterone, probably not. For a small libido bump or as a cooking spice it is a low-risk option. It may be a small help if your blood sugar runs high.
entries.dose_text: Seed extract ~500-600 mg a day.
entries.forms: Seed extract (what was studied); plain seed powder is used in larger amounts. Match the label to the study form.
entries.cycling: 6-12 weeks.
entries.interactions: Lowers blood sugar with diabetes medicine (watch for shakiness, sweating, confusion). May thin the blood. Avoid in pregnancy (may cause contractions) and with a peanut or chickpea allergy.
entries.side_effects: Maple-syrup smell in sweat or urine (harmless); stomach upset, gas, loose stool; can lower potassium in some people.
entries.source: 05.11.03 Fadogia, Tribulus and Fenugreek; 05.11.01 Testosterone Boosters - What Can and Can't Work; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Maca
entries.verdict_text: 'Safest for desire and mood'; 'does not raise testosterone'
entries.why: Worth a try for desire (men and women), not for erection trouble or low T. Small trials show effects on desire (not hormone-driven); mood is mixed; placebo may explain part.
entries.dose_text: About 1.5-3 g of maca powder a day.
entries.forms: Powder or capsule; gelatinized maca is gentler on the stomach.
entries.timing: Avoid late in the day (trouble sleeping).
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks (about two to three months).
entries.interactions: With a thyroid problem, check with a pharmacist (cabbage family). Avoid with hormone-sensitive cancers.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset, bloating or gas, trouble sleeping if taken late, jitters or faster heartbeat in some.
entries.source: 05.11.04 Shilajit, Maca and Other Herbal Boosters; 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Shilajit (purified)
entries.verdict_text: 'Clearest testosterone signal' — but needs a tested, purified product
entries.why: A few small trials (one placebo-controlled) showed a rise in testosterone and energy, but nothing independently repeated: not strong enough to promise a result. Raw shilajit can contain lead, arsenic, mercury and mold.
entries.dose_text: About 250-500 mg a day of purified shilajit.
entries.forms: Purified or processed product with a recent certificate of analysis showing metals below safe limits, third-party tested (USP Verified), and a clear dose. Avoid raw resin.
entries.cycling: Several weeks; one-herb trial of 8-12 weeks.
entries.interactions: Avoid with pregnancy or breastfeeding, conditions where extra iron is harmful (hemochromatosis), or kidney problems.
entries.side_effects: Heavy metals in raw product harm nerves, kidneys and blood. Fulvic acid is not a proven testosterone raiser.
entries.contradictions: 05.11.04 calls it 'the clearest testosterone signal of the five'; 05.14.07 (trending) says 'Weak proof, with a real contamination risk … not a place to gamble'.
entries.source: 05.11.04 Shilajit, Maca and Other Herbal Boosters; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Mucuna pruriens (velvet bean)
entries.why: Acts like a drug (L-dopa). A plausible mechanism and a few small studies in infertile men, but not enough to say it works for testosterone; nothing shows a rise in healthy men.
entries.dose_text: Studies used several grams of seed powder a day, not standardized. Start low; check the L-dopa percent.
entries.interactions: Do not combine with Parkinson's drugs, MAOIs (dangerous BP spike), antipsychotics, other antidepressants or BP medicine. Avoid with pregnancy or breastfeeding, a history of psychosis or serious mood problems, melanoma or a changing mole.
entries.side_effects: Nausea, headache, restlessness, insomnia, low BP and dizziness, mood changes, hallucinations at high doses.
entries.source: 05.11.04 Shilajit, Maca and Other Herbal Boosters; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Horny goat weed (Epimedium / icariin)
entries.why: Good human trials are almost absent; the PDE5 block is lab and animal only, with no proof it raises T. It is often a vehicle for hidden drugs (spiked with sildenafil).
entries.interactions: Check with a pharmacist if on BP, heart or erection medicine. Avoid with heart rhythm problems or hormone-sensitive conditions.
entries.side_effects: Racing heart, nosebleeds or dizziness at high doses.
entries.source: 05.11.04 Shilajit, Maca and Other Herbal Boosters; 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Stinging nettle root
entries.why: There is no good proof of a testosterone effect: it binds SHBG only in test tubes. Human trials are mostly small ones for prostate symptoms. Its 'natural aromatase inhibitor' evidence is also weak.
entries.interactions: May lower BP or blood sugar; may add to water pills and blood thinners. Avoid in pregnancy.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset.
entries.source: 05.11.04 Shilajit, Maca and Other Herbal Boosters; 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone)
entries.verdict_text: Helps a little in specific groups; 'weak' in healthy men; banned in most tested sports
entries.why: DHEA is a real hormone. It may make sense for confirmed adrenal insufficiency on replacement, or an older woman with truly low DHEA-S and matching symptoms (modest lumbar BMD rise). For healthy people chasing energy, fat loss or longevity the proof is weak, and it is not a stand-in for treating low T.
entries.dose_text: Studied doses ('not a prescription'): adrenal insufficiency 25-50 mg a day; women ~5-25 mg a day; older men mostly 50-100 mg a day (weak gains, no set dose). Start at the low end; more is not better.
entries.forms: OTC in the US, prescription-only or controlled in many countries; potency is often wrong, so use USP Verified or NSF Certified. Prasterone (prescription vaginal DHEA) is not the same as a pill.
entries.cycling: Retest after several weeks at a steady dose; if levels climb above where they should, stop and retest.
test_first: fasting insulin and glucose (if diabetes risk)
entries.interactions: Check any prescription with a pharmacist. Does not fit hormone-sensitive cancer, pregnancy, or young healthy 'optimization'. Banned in most tested sports. Pause it before the baseline draw and stop biotin 48-72 h before.
entries.side_effects: Women: acne, oily skin, scalp hair thinning, facial or body hair, deeper voice (if your voice changes, stop; it may last). Men: breast tenderness or swelling, water retention.
entries.source: 05.11.05 DHEA and Pregnenolone; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Pregnenolone
entries.why: There is no proven use for healthy people, and taking more at the top does not reliably raise any hormone below it. If the plan is 'I'm just going to try it', pass. 'Pregnenolone steal' is an oversimplification.
entries.dose_text: Trials used 25-500 mg; no accepted dose.
test_first: the hormone you care about (testosterone, estradiol, cortisol)
entries.interactions: Avoid with hormone-sensitive cancer or higher prostate-cancer risk; a poor idea in pregnancy.
entries.source: 05.11.05 DHEA and Pregnenolone; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: DIM (diindolylmethane)
entries.verdict_text: 'Has not been shown to lower blood estradiol'
entries.why: A low-payoff product with mild side effects. It is not an estrogen blocker: it shifts urinary metabolites only. Treat it as a small side experiment on top of fat loss and less alcohol.
entries.dose_text: Labels give 100-300 mg a day; there is no proven dose.
entries.forms: Single ingredient with the dose per capsule, third-party tested. Avoid 'estrogen balance' blends. Food first: cruciferous vegetables a few times a week.
entries.cycling: A fair test of a couple of months, then retest estradiol; if nothing changed, stop.
entries.interactions: Can change how the liver handles medicines. Do not add it on your own with tamoxifen, birth control, an aromatase inhibitor or past hormone-sensitive cancer. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset, nausea, headache.
entries.source: 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: I3C (indole-3-carbinol)
entries.verdict_text: No reason to pick it over DIM
entries.why: It converts to DIM in the stomach and can upset the stomach more.
entries.source: 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'

entries.name: Calcium D-glucarate
entries.why: Lab and animal data only. Your liver and gut already clear estrogen, so the 'detox' framing is unnecessary; fiber and plants are better.
entries.dose_text: Labels often give 500-1,500 mg a day; there is no proven dose.
entries.side_effects: Seems well tolerated; long-term safety is not well studied.
entries.source: 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 'Natural aromatase inhibitors' / estrogen-blocker blends (chrysin, etc.)
entries.verdict_text: The evidence for them is weak
entries.why: Do not rely on any of them if you have a truly high estradiol. They carry an adulteration risk (steroids, stimulants, unlisted drugs).
entries.source: 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'

entries.name: Aromatase inhibitors bought online ('research chemicals', e.g. anastrozole)
entries.why: Prescription drugs. Doctors use very small doses only when estradiol is clearly high on a sensitive test and causing symptoms. Online 'research chemicals' have unknown doses and contents.
entries.side_effects: Too-low estradiol in men: joint pain, low sex drive, erection trouble, low mood, poorer cholesterol, weaker bones.
entries.source: 05.11.06 DIM, Calcium D-Glucarate and 'Estrogen Blockers'; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Yohimbine / yohimbe bark
entries.why: Skip it: the risk is not worth a small gain (some trials show a modest erection gain; the fat-loss effect is small and inconsistent), and the helpful dose is close to the harmful dose. Bark products are often mislabeled.
entries.dose_text: As used for fat loss: about 0.2 mg per kg body weight, usually fasted.
entries.interactions: Dangerous with MAO inhibitors and other stimulants. Risky with high blood pressure, anxiety disorders or heart disease. US tablets are prescription-only.
entries.side_effects: Anxiety, jitters, panic, racing heart, high BP spikes. Chest pain, pounding heartbeat, fainting or severe headache with high BP: stop and get help fast.
entries.source: 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 'Male enhancement' / 'natural Viagra' blends
entries.verdict_text: 'The most dangerous corner of the supplement aisle'
entries.why: Never take a pill sold as 'enhancement' with an unknown label. They often hide sildenafil, tadalafil or similar at unknown, possibly higher-than-prescription doses; other blend doses are hidden and usually too low to matter.
entries.interactions: Hidden PDE5 drugs plus nitrates cause a dangerous BP drop.
entries.side_effects: Erection >4 hours; chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath during sex; sudden vision or hearing loss: emergency.
entries.source: 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections; 05.06.03 Buying Supplements; 05.11.02 Tongkat Ali; 05.11.04 Shilajit, Maca and Other Herbal Boosters

entries.name: Prescription PDE5 drugs (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil)
entries.why: A prescription erection pill is not the villain; a clinician checks BP and medicines first. ED can precede heart symptoms by ~3 years on average, so get checked.
entries.interactions: Anyone who takes nitrates should not use them. They add to the BP drop from citrulline, arginine and beetroot.
entries.source: 05.11.07 Supplements for Libido and Erections

entries.name: Omega-3 fish oil (EPA + DHA)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: Tier 1 foundation, if you eat little fish
entries.why: Strong for triglycerides (~6 mg/dL drop per extra gram; 3-4 g/day cuts TG 20-50%) and for raising your Omega-3 Index. Likely helpful for people at high heart risk on high doses. It is modest or unproven for healthy people trying to prevent a first heart problem (VITAL/ASCEND at ~1 g/day showed no cut), so do not take it expecting to prevent a heart attack.
entries.dose_text: General health / raise the index: about 1-2 g a day EPA plus DHA (~2 g/day moves an index of 4% toward 8% in 3-4 months). High triglycerides: 2-4 g a day EPA+DHA. Count EPA+DHA, not 'fish oil': a 1,000 mg softgel often holds ~300 mg EPA+DHA (2 g/day ≈ 7 × 300 mg or ~3 × 600 mg softgels). Pregnancy: at least 200-300 mg DHA a day.
entries.forms: Triglyceride (TG) or re-esterified triglyceride (rTG) absorbs better. Ethyl ester (EE) is cheapest but absorbed less, especially without a fatty meal (an unstated form is probably EE). Look for IFOS certification, low TOTOX, added tocopherols, and small cold-water fish. A strong fishy smell or taste means oxidation: throw it out. Refrigerate once opened.
entries.timing: With a meal that has fat (without fat absorption can drop by about half); the biggest meal is a good choice. Split across two meals for fishy burps.
entries.cycling: Take daily for 3-4 months, then retest. If 8-12%, stay there; if under 8%, raise the dose or add fatty fish. Above 3 g/day, use a prescription form with lab tracking.
entries.interactions: Thins the blood a little at high doses: take care with warfarin or antiplatelet drugs and check with a pharmacist. Tell the surgical team before surgery. It adds to the bleeding effect of nattokinase, chondroitin, curcumin and ginkgo.
entries.side_effects: Fishy burps, mild stomach upset or loose stools. Slightly raises atrial fibrillation risk, more at higher doses. At ≥4 g/day it can raise LDL a little in some people with high TG (DHA-rich more than EPA). A racing or uneven heartbeat, chest pain, bleeding that won't stop or black stools: get care fast.
entries.contradictions: High-triglyceride dose: 05.06.02 says 3-4 g a day EPA+DHA; 05.12.01 and the cheat sheet give the treatment range as 2-4 g a day.
entries.source: 05.06.02 The Short List; 05.06.04 How to Read a Label; 05.06.05 Test First; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.12.01 Omega-3 Fish Oil; 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Icosapent ethyl (prescription purified EPA)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: High-risk people had fewer heart events (REDUCE-IT); the placebo debate is not settled
entries.why: In REDUCE-IT, 4 g a day meant fewer heart events in high-risk people, but some experts think part of the gain came from the mineral-oil placebo. It is the prescription form for doses above 3 g a day (the AHA backs 4 g a day prescription omega-3 for high triglycerides).
entries.dose_text: 4 g a day (prescription).
entries.source: 05.12.01 Omega-3 Fish Oil

entries.name: Krill oil
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Each have their caveats' — a fine choice if you tolerate it better
entries.why: Omega-3 bound to phospholipids and absorbed well, but each capsule holds a lower dose and costs more per gram of EPA+DHA. You still need to count the milligrams.
entries.dose_text: Count EPA+DHA to the fish-oil targets (1-2 g a day).
entries.source: 05.12.01 Omega-3 Fish Oil; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Algae oil (vegan omega-3)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: The vegan or vegetarian route to EPA+DHA, and also an option for DHA in pregnancy. Most are mostly DHA with some EPA, so check the label for both.
entries.dose_text: At least 250-500 mg EPA+DHA per serving; pregnancy ≥200-300 mg DHA a day.
entries.timing: With a meal that has fat.
entries.cycling: Test the Omega-3 Index in 3-4 months.
entries.source: 05.12.01 Omega-3 Fish Oil; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Cod liver oil
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: Skip in pregnancy (vitamin A); not for high dosing
entries.why: It also carries vitamin A and vitamin D. Do not use it to reach a high omega-3 dose, because vitamin A builds up in the body.
entries.interactions: Counts toward the preformed vitamin A upper limit (3,000 mcg RAE). Many agencies advise avoiding it in pregnancy.
entries.source: 05.12.01 Omega-3 Fish Oil; 05.07.06 Vitamins A and E; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Flaxseed / chia / walnut ALA (as an EPA/DHA substitute)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: Does not raise your index much
entries.why: Only a few percent of ALA converts to EPA and DHA (some people convert less because of FADS1/FADS2 genes), so flax, chia and walnuts are food, not a fish-oil substitute.
entries.source: 05.12.01 Omega-3 Fish Oil

entries.name: Berberine (HCl)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Nature's Ozempic' is marketing; may help prediabetes, T2D, metabolic syndrome, PCOS
entries.why: Genuinely useful for blood sugar and lipid markers in people whose numbers are off: fasting glucose down ~10-15 mg/dL and HbA1c down ~0.6 points, roughly matching metformin in some trials. It is not a miracle or a fat burner; the weight effect is small at best. With normal glucose, HbA1c and insulin there is little to fix.
entries.dose_text: 500 mg, two or three times a day (1,000-1,500 mg total). Start with 500 mg once a day with the largest meal in week 1, then add a second dose; add a third only if needed and your stomach agrees.
entries.forms: Berberine HCl, the most studied form, with milligrams stated and third-party testing. Avoid goldenseal-based products and 'metabolic' blends that hide the amount.
entries.timing: Each dose with or just before a meal that has carbohydrates; skip the dose at a meal with almost no carbs.
entries.cycling: No strong proof that continuous use or pausing is better. Retest at 8-12 weeks; if the numbers haven't moved, stop.
entries.interactions: Blocks CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, raising levels of statins, cyclosporine, some calcium-channel blockers and many others; check with a pharmacist. With insulin, sulfonylureas or other glucose-lowering drugs there is a hypoglycemia risk, so plan first. Do not stack with red yeast rice or a statin. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding (bilirubin displacement); never give it to newborns or infants. Extra care with liver disease.
entries.side_effects: Diarrhea, cramping, constipation and nausea (dose-dependent). Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, severe belly pain, or low sugar that doesn't improve after eating: stop and get care.
entries.source: 05.12.02 Berberine; 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Dihydroberberine
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: A changed form of berberine that the body absorbs better. The evidence is thinner than for regular berberine but the idea makes sense, and it can suit people who can't tolerate the standard form's stomach effects.
entries.dose_text: Often 100-200 mg twice a day.
entries.interactions: Do not combine with regular berberine at full dose. Same drug-interaction cautions as berberine.
entries.source: 05.12.02 Berberine; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Goldenseal (as a berberine source)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Goldenseal-based products tend to carry less berberine, and the plant is overharvested.
entries.source: 05.12.02 Berberine

entries.name: Proprietary 'metabolic' / blood-sugar blends
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Blends of berberine, chromium, cinnamon, green tea and the like often hold each ingredient at too low a dose to do anything, and they may hide the amounts.
entries.source: 05.12.02 Berberine

entries.name: Psyllium husk
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: If you only try one fiber supplement, make it psyllium. It lowers LDL (~2.2 mg/dL per gram of soluble fiber, so 5-10 g ≈ 5-10%), helps regularity in either direction and aids fullness. The LDL drop is modest and not a replacement for a statin when one is needed.
entries.dose_text: Studied range 5-10 g a day of psyllium, split into two doses, each with ~8 oz water. Fiber targets: ~25 g a day women, ~38 g men.
entries.forms: Powder or whole husk, single ingredient (cheapest and easiest to hit a real dose). Capsules hold little fiber each. Avoid wafers and gummies (little fiber, extra sugar) and versions with added sugar or dyes.
entries.timing: Mix in water or a smoothie and drink right away before it thickens. Separate from medicines (e.g. thyroid pills) by a couple of hours.
entries.cycling: Ramp up: days 1-3 half dose once a day; days 4-7 half dose twice; week 2 full dose split in two. Stay with it 6-12 weeks before judging.
entries.interactions: Can reduce absorption of some medicines. Do not use it if you have trouble swallowing, slow stomach emptying or a history of bowel blockage. With IBS, start small.
entries.side_effects: Gas, bloating and cramps if started too fast. With too little water it can block the throat or gut. Severe belly pain with swelling, vomiting with no gas or stool, or food stuck in the throat: get care.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others; 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Glucomannan (konjac)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: A small, honest job if used right: a pound or two over several weeks with a calorie deficit. It is not a fat burner. It can also lower cholesterol and blood sugar a little.
entries.dose_text: About 1 g, 15-30 minutes before meals, with a full glass of water or two; up to about 3 g a day total in studies.
entries.forms: Powder in plenty of water, or capsules with a full glass, is safer. Dry tablets have been linked to choking.
entries.timing: 15-30 minutes before meals; take your pills at least an hour before it. Start low.
entries.interactions: Avoid with trouble swallowing or a narrowed gut.
entries.side_effects: Gas and bloating, which fade with time. Choking or blockage if taken with too little water.
entries.contradictions: Medicine spacing: 05.12.07 says take pills at least an hour before glucomannan; 05.12.03 says separate fiber from medicines by a couple of hours.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others; 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Prebiotics: inulin / FOS / GOS
entries.why: They feed gut bacteria and raise Bifidobacteria, but the catch is gas. Mixed fiber from food and resistant starch are gentler for most people.
entries.dose_text: Start with 3-5 g a day and build slowly.
entries.interactions: With IBS or FODMAP sensitivity, fermentable fibers can make symptoms worse.
entries.side_effects: Bloating and cramps, worse at higher doses.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others; 05.14.01 Probiotics; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Partially hydrolyzed guar gum (PHGG)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Many people find it easier on the gut: a fair pick if other fibers give you trouble, and gentle bulk with little gas. With IBS, try psyllium or PHGG in small amounts first.
entries.dose_text: Not stated; ramp slowly.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Resistant starch powder (raw potato starch, RS2)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Positive for stool bulk and butyrate, but individual results vary a lot: some feel better, others just get bloated. It must not be cooked, since heat destroys the resistant part.
entries.dose_text: 1-2 tablespoons stirred into a cold drink ≈ 8-16 g resistant starch; studies in healthy adults used ~22-45 g a day.
entries.timing: In a cold drink; never cooked.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Methylcellulose
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: A quiet option for people who bloat with everything else. It does not lower cholesterol the way psyllium does.
entries.dose_text: Not stated.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Wheat bran
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: Not a first pick for IBS
entries.why: Insoluble fiber that speeds transit. It can irritate sensitive guts.
entries.interactions: High bran intake can lower iron and zinc absorption.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others

entries.name: 'Gut cleanse' / detox fiber blends
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Long 'gut cleanse' blends with detox promises add cost and nothing else.
entries.source: 05.12.03 Fiber Supplements - Psyllium and Others; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money

entries.name: Plant sterols / stanols
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: LDL ~8-10% lower — 'one of the best-supported add-ons after food and fiber'
entries.why: About 2 g a day lowers LDL roughly 8-10% with small side effects; sterols come first among the heart add-ons. No large trial has shown they cut heart attacks, and they do little for triglycerides.
entries.dose_text: About 2 g a day with a meal; more than ~2-3 g a day adds little. Food gives only a few hundred mg.
entries.forms: Fortified spreads, drinks, yogurt drinks, chews or softgels; read the grams per serving (you may need 2-3 servings).
entries.timing: With a meal (ideally with some fat), every day. The effect fades within weeks if you stop.
entries.cycling: Retest at 6-12 weeks.
entries.interactions: Stacks with a statin and diet changes. People with sitosterolemia should avoid them.
entries.side_effects: Can lower blood carotenoids such as beta-carotene; fruit and vegetables help balance this.
entries.source: 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Red yeast rice (monacolin K)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Dose is uncontrolled'; carries statin risks — 'Look at a prescription first'
entries.why: Red yeast rice is not like a statin; it contains one (monacolin K = lovastatin). It is an unregulated, weaker, less certain version of the same idea. It may fit someone with mildly high LDL who wants to avoid a prescription statin and is not already on one. A 2024 Japan incident linked one maker's products to serious kidney damage and deaths.
entries.dose_text: There is no single standard dose; labels showing only total red yeast rice may hold nearly nothing or a real statin dose.
entries.forms: If used: a stated monacolin K amount plus a citrinin test, a third-party seal or batch report. Do not trust 'citrinin-free' claims with no proof.
entries.cycling: Stop if LDL doesn't fall or any muscle pain appears.
entries.interactions: Never with a prescription statin. Not with berberine without guidance ('Do not stack red yeast rice, berberine and a statin together'). Grapefruit raises lovastatin; some antibiotics, antifungals, heart and immune drugs interact. Heavy alcohol adds liver risk. Skip with pregnancy, trying to conceive, breastfeeding, liver disease, past statin muscle trouble, or in children. Check local legality.
entries.side_effects: Muscle aches, weakness, dark tea-colored urine, rare rhabdomyolysis; raised liver enzymes; citrinin contamination (a kidney toxin). Severe muscle pain, dark urine or yellow skin: get care.
entries.source: 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Bergamot (citrus flavonoid extract)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Small, short trials with different products show a modest drop in LDL and TG, with no outcome trials.
entries.forms: A product listing the bergamot extract amount and flavonoid content, third-party tested (not the peel oil used for Earl Grey).
entries.cycling: Retest lipids after 6-12 weeks.
entries.interactions: It is a citrus like grapefruit, so check prescriptions with a pharmacist.
entries.source: 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Garlic supplements (aged garlic extract, powder, oil)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: The supplement is a minor add-on at best: small drops in total cholesterol and blood pressure, and it has not been shown to prevent heart attacks. For immunity there are some small studies, nothing strong.
entries.interactions: Makes blood less sticky, so check if you take a blood thinner or have surgery coming (high-dose garlic is flagged before surgery). It can lower levels of some HIV medicines and adds to nattokinase's bleeding risk.
entries.side_effects: Garlic breath, body odor, heartburn; higher doses can upset the stomach.
entries.source: 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Nattokinase
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Thin evidence with a real bleeding risk'
entries.why: A few short trials show slight BP drops, mixed cholesterol results and no outcome trials. Do not self-treat a clot risk with a supplement.
entries.dose_text: Listed in FU (fibrinolytic units); no amount stated.
entries.interactions: Warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, high-dose fish oil, garlic and other blood-thinning supplements. Stop before surgery. Avoid with a soy allergy or bleeding disorder.
entries.source: 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Hawthorn (leaf, flower, berry)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Modest, mostly a risk for people on heart drugs'
entries.why: Studied as an add-on in mild to moderate heart failure, with small BP drops. It does little for LDL.
entries.interactions: With digoxin, nitrates or beta-blockers it can slow the heart or drop BP too far; check any heart or BP drug with a pharmacist.
entries.side_effects: Chest pain, racing heart, fainting or shortness of breath need a doctor fast; don't use supplements in their place.
entries.source: 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 'Cholesterol support' blends
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Do not use 'cholesterol support' blends with hidden amounts.
entries.source: 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements

entries.name: CoQ10 (ubiquinone / ubiquinol)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: Heart failure 'Maybe worth it'; statin aches 'Worth a trial'; migraine 'Optional'; healthy 'Probably not worth it'
entries.why: A 'maybe' supplement for a few specific cases, not a daily must-have. Strongest in heart failure (Q-SYMBIO ~300 mg/day for 2 years: fewer major events and deaths), always as an add-on to medicine. Mixed for statin aches (the 2018 US cholesterol guideline does not recommend it). It does not lower LDL. Probably not worth it for energy or anti-aging in healthy people.
entries.dose_text: Usual range 100-300 mg a day; 100-200 mg for general use or a statin trial; ~300 mg a day in the heart-failure trial.
entries.forms: Ubiquinone is the standard, cheaper form and enough for many. Ubiquinol absorbs a bit better, especially in older adults or non-responders. An oil-based softgel stating form and mg, third-party tested; avoid 'antioxidant complex' blends and high-priced 'bioavailable' versions.
entries.timing: With a meal that has fat; split doses above 100-200 mg (breakfast and dinner); morning or lunch preferred, since it can be stimulating late.
entries.cycling: Give it 6-8 weeks for muscle symptoms and longer for migraines. If nothing changed, stop; you don't need to take it forever.
entries.interactions: Resembles vitamin K and can make warfarin work less well; don't start without an INR check. Additive BP drop with BP medicine; watch for lows on diabetes medicine. With cancer treatment, check with a pharmacist. Skip in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Don't quit a statin on your own.
entries.side_effects: Mild and uncommon: upset stomach, nausea, loose stools, trouble sleeping if taken late, rarely headache or rash. No serious harm shown at usual doses.
entries.source: 05.12.05 CoQ10; 05.12.04 Red Yeast Rice, Plant Sterols and Other Heart Supplements; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Myo-inositol (incl. 40:1 myo : D-chiro)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: A low-risk extra for women with PCOS and insulin resistance, not a stand-in for metformin or other proven treatment (the 2023 PCOS guideline rated evidence 'limited and inconclusive'). Thin evidence for high fasting insulin and very little research in men. Fat loss is still the strongest move in PCOS.
entries.dose_text: 2-4 g a day is the usual range (guideline trials 1.2-4 g a day); 40:1 mix ~4 g a day total. With selenium: myo-inositol 600 mg + selenium 83 mcg twice daily lowered TPO antibodies more than selenium alone in some studies.
entries.forms: Powder mixes in water and tastes slightly sweet; capsules need many pills to reach 2 g.
entries.timing: Split into two servings, morning and evening.
entries.cycling: At least 3 months; keep a period diary.
entries.interactions: Watch for low blood sugar on diabetes medicine. Tested in pregnancy without clear harm (data limited); tell your prenatal team.
entries.side_effects: Well tolerated; higher amounts can cause nausea, gas or loose stools.
entries.source: 05.12.06 Inositol, Chromium, Cinnamon and Apple Cider Vinegar; 05.08.04 Iodine and Selenium; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Chromium (e.g. chromium picolinate)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Small, often none'; 'skip it if blood sugar is normal'
entries.why: Helps mostly if you are low, and a real shortage is very rare (no reliable test exists). Reviews call the effect small at best. In type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, already on a diet and training plan, it is a low-risk extra to test. It does not melt fat or build muscle.
entries.dose_text: Studies used ~200-1,000 mcg a day; adult need ~20-35 mcg a day. More is not better; no firm upper limit has been set.
entries.forms: Studies often used chromium picolinate.
entries.cycling: Run for 3 months and compare HbA1c and fasting glucose; stop if no change.
entries.interactions: Can lower blood sugar: watch for lows on insulin or diabetes pills. Many multivitamins already contain it, so check before stacking.
entries.side_effects: Usually well tolerated; rare reports link very high doses to kidney or liver trouble, skin or stomach upset.
entries.source: 05.12.06 Inositol, Chromium, Cinnamon and Apple Cider Vinegar; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: A flavor that might do a tiny bit extra (a small drop in fasting glucose; HbA1c barely moves), not a treatment, and only the Ceylon kind. Not proven for weight loss.
entries.dose_text: Trials used 1-6 g a day (up to ~2 teaspoons). Coumarin limit ~0.1 mg per kg body weight (7 mg for a 70 kg adult).
entries.forms: Ceylon (very little coumarin). A label that only says 'cinnamon' is nearly always cassia.
entries.cycling: Check HbA1c and fasting glucose after 3 months.
entries.interactions: Avoid with liver disease or high ALT and liver-stressing medicines. On diabetes medicine, monitor glucose.
entries.side_effects: Do not take it by the spoonful: inhaling the powder harms the lungs.
entries.source: 05.12.06 Inositol, Chromium, Cinnamon and Apple Cider Vinegar; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Cassia cinnamon (daily / capsules)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: Avoid for daily or supplement use
entries.why: A label that only says 'cinnamon' is nearly always cassia. Cassia has a lot of coumarin, which can hurt the liver or raise liver enzymes (reversible when stopped). A level teaspoon can hold the ~0.1 mg/kg daily coumarin limit or more. Fine only as a small food spice.
entries.source: 05.12.06 Inositol, Chromium, Cinnamon and Apple Cider Vinegar; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Apple cider vinegar (liquid)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Small and short' drop in post-meal sugar
entries.why: Small studies show a small, short drop in post-meal blood sugar, with little change in fasting glucose or HbA1c. It does not melt fat, 'cleanse' or 'detox', fix heartburn, or boost stomach acid ('no real evidence').
entries.dose_text: About 1-2 tablespoons (15-30 mL) diluted in at least 8 oz water.
entries.timing: Just before or with a meal that has a lot of carbs. Never drink it straight: use a straw, rinse with water, and wait 30 minutes before brushing.
entries.interactions: Avoid with acid reflux, a sensitive stomach or gastroparesis. Extra glucose lowering with insulin or diabetes pills. With diuretics or heart pills that lower potassium, long-term large amounts are linked to low potassium.
entries.side_effects: Tooth enamel erosion, throat irritation, can worsen heartburn.
entries.source: 05.12.06 Inositol, Chromium, Cinnamon and Apple Cider Vinegar; 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Apple cider vinegar gummies / tablets
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'No vinegar tablets'; ACV gummies hold far less acetic acid
entries.why: Tablets can stick in the throat and burn it. Gummies hold very little vinegar (some almost none) and mostly give you sugar and a nice label. The studies used liquid; weight-loss and detox claims are not backed.
entries.source: 05.12.06 Inositol, Chromium, Cinnamon and Apple Cider Vinegar; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Green tea extract (concentrated EGCG)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: 'Drink coffee and green tea, skip the extract.'
entries.why: The upside is tiny (a pound or two over several months in the better results; many trials find almost nothing, mostly from added caffeine) and the downside is a liver: EGCG ≥~800 mg a day raised liver enzymes, with serious cases reported. Brewed tea does not carry the same risk.
entries.dose_text: If you try it anyway, stay well under 800 mg EGCG a day.
entries.timing: With food; an empty stomach raises the risk.
entries.interactions: Avoid with liver trouble, frequent alcohol or other liver-stressing products.
entries.side_effects: Liver injury. Dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, right-sided belly pain, or deep tiredness with nausea: stop and get seen.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: CLA (conjugated linoleic acid)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: A very small loss of body fat, well under a pound a month on average, and it does not clearly help muscle.
entries.dose_text: Studied ~3-6 g a day.
entries.side_effects: Upset stomach, loose stools, fatigue; some studies found higher liver fat or worse insulin resistance in some people.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Garcinia cambogia (HCA)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Little to no weight loss beyond placebo, with liver injury cases reported: not worth any risk to your liver.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Raspberry ketones
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: Almost no good human trials. Effective animal doses are far above any label, and any felt effect usually comes from added caffeine.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Synephrine (bitter orange)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: It raises calorie burn a little and can lower hunger, but the fat-loss gain is small and the risk is not. Some sports groups ban it.
entries.interactions: Caffeine adds to its heart-rate and BP effects; it can interact with some medicines.
entries.side_effects: Raised heart rate and BP; a steady rise or new palpitations means stop.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: ECA stack (ephedrine + caffeine + aspirin) / ephedra
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.verdict_text: Raises HR and BP; tied to serious heart events
entries.why: About three-quarters of the effect is appetite suppression, so 'fires up your metabolism' is mostly false. Ephedrine stacks have been tied to serious heart events. Ephedra was banned as a US supplement in 2004, and ephedrine is limited in the US and banned in sport above a set level.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Fat burners (incl. stimulant stacks and spiked products)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: At best a fat burner adds a few dozen calories of burn a day, about five almonds. Layered stimulants buy a faster heart, more anxiety and worse sleep, not more fat loss. Products are often spiked with hidden drugs (sibutramine, pulled for raising heart attack and stroke risk; the old laxative phenolphthalein; antidepressants; unlisted stimulants). What works: a small calorie gap, ~0.8 g/lb protein, lifting 3-4×/week, steps and sleep; coffee is the cheap extra.
entries.interactions: Hidden drugs are dangerous with prescriptions. Avoid in pregnancy and for teens. Two or more marketing red flags: skip. Skip any fat burner that hides its doses.
entries.side_effects: Racing heart, bad sleep, liver risk. Chest pain, pounding or uneven heartbeat, fainting, or severe headache with high BP: stop and get help fast.
entries.source: 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.06.03 Buying Supplements; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol)
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: It makes your body overheat. There is no antidote, people have died, and it has no safe use for weight loss.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Clenbuterol and other beta-2 agonist pills
entries.category: Heart, blood sugar and fat loss
entries.why: These are drugs, banned in sport, with real heart risks. They are not supplements.
entries.source: 05.12.07 Fat Burners - Green Tea Extract, CLA, Carnitine and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide)
entries.verdict_text: 'Pick one, not both'; no lifespan trial
entries.why: If you are healthy, NMN is an expensive experiment. It reliably raises a number in blood but has not been shown to help people live longer or better; lifespan stories come from mice. The best signal is better muscle insulin response in women with overweight and prediabetes.
entries.dose_text: Studied range 250-900 mg a day (250 mg a day for 10 weeks in prediabetes; 300-900 mg a day for 60 days in healthy adults; up to 1,250 mg a day for four weeks tolerated). A middle dose is a sensible start; more is not better, and no trial shows loading works better.
entries.forms: Beta-NMN (often as a chloride salt); plain capsules or powder are fine. Sublingual and liposomal forms are unproven and cost more. Avoid proprietary blends. It is fragile: keep it cool and dry. Third-party tested (USP Verified, NSF Certified for Sport).
entries.timing: No proven best time; many take it in the morning with food.
entries.cycling: Set a limit (e.g. 12 weeks); recheck your chosen number after three months; if nothing moved, stop.
test_first: pre-set number (blood pressure, fasting glucose or walking test)
entries.interactions: Do not stack with NR (redundant). Skip if pregnant or breastfeeding, or with current or past cancer. Check prescriptions with a pharmacist. High-dose users may add a B-complex.
entries.side_effects: Mild: upset stomach, bloating, nausea, headache. Long-term safety is unknown.
entries.source: 05.13.01 NAD Boosters - NMN and NR; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: NR (nicotinamide riboside)
entries.verdict_text: 'More human trials' — the safer pick of the NAD boosters
entries.why: An expensive experiment for healthy people, but if you want the form with more human data, NR is the safer pick. It raises blood NAD+ ~60%; the clearest signal is small drops in BP and artery stiffness in people who started higher. It did not improve insulin sensitivity. No lifespan proof.
entries.dose_text: 250-500 mg twice a day (500-1,000 mg a day) for 6-12 weeks in older adults; up to 2,000 mg a day for 12 weeks tolerated.
entries.forms: NR chloride (used in most studies); plain capsules or powder are fine.
entries.timing: Morning with food is common; no proven best time.
entries.cycling: ~12-week limit, then judge your pre-set number.
test_first: pre-set number (blood pressure, fasting glucose or walking test)
entries.interactions: Do not stack with NMN. Skip with pregnancy, breastfeeding or cancer. High doses have had mixed effects on homocysteine; some add a B-complex.
entries.side_effects: Mild: upset stomach, bloating, nausea, headache.
entries.source: 05.13.01 NAD Boosters - NMN and NR; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: NAD+ IV drips / shots (and oral NAD+)
entries.verdict_text: 'No proven dose and thinner proof than pills'
entries.why: No large, well-run trial has proven a dose for drips or shots; any dosing you see is a guess. Oral NAD+ itself is chopped up in the gut, which is why precursors exist.
entries.interactions: People with unstable heart disease or serious lung disease should not use drips; also skip with pregnancy, breastfeeding or cancer. Use only a licensed clinic.
entries.side_effects: Mostly from running too fast: flushing, nausea, chest pressure or trouble breathing, headache; also sore vein, infection or a bad batch. If chest pain, racing heart or trouble breathing starts, tell staff to stop it right away.
entries.source: 05.13.01 NAD Boosters - NMN and NR; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: NADH
entries.why: Small, older trials in fatigue and Parkinson's were too small to prove much.
entries.source: 05.13.01 NAD Boosters - NMN and NR

entries.name: Resveratrol
entries.why: 'Skip it … a marketing fossil.' It is absorbed and then broken down fast, and other options have far better proof for metabolic and heart goals.
entries.dose_text: Studies used ~100 mg to several grams a day.
