entries.interactions: Can change how the liver handles some prescriptions (e.g. blood thinners). Skip with pregnancy, breastfeeding or cancer.
entries.side_effects: Upset stomach, nausea, diarrhea at high doses; long-term high-dose safety unknown.
entries.source: 05.13.02 Resveratrol, Spermidine, Fisetin and Quercetin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Spermidine
entries.verdict_text: Most reasonable of the four; 'None is a core part of a plan'
entries.why: Early promise, little proof: no human lifespan evidence, and a year-long trial found no memory benefit. The easy win is to eat the foods that contain it (wheat germ, aged cheese, mushrooms, natto, legumes).
entries.dose_text: Most supplements give ~1 to a few mg a day (no more than, and often less than, a diet rich in those foods).
entries.forms: Wheat germ extract with a clear source.
entries.cycling: Fair test: write down a number first, run ~8-12 weeks, stop if it didn't move.
test_first: one pre-set number (hs-CRP, fasting glucose, BP, strength test or sleep)
entries.interactions: Skip with past or current cancer, pregnancy or breastfeeding. With wheat allergy or celiac, read the ingredient line.
entries.side_effects: Mild in trials; long-term safety unknown.
entries.source: 05.13.02 Resveratrol, Spermidine, Fisetin and Quercetin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Fisetin
entries.why: Weak human proof with trials still running: an experiment at best. 'Hit and run' senolytic schedules come from mouse work; do not copy a schedule off a forum. Clearing senescent cells hard or often has not been studied long term.
entries.interactions: Skip with pregnancy, breastfeeding or cancer; check blood thinners with a pharmacist.
entries.source: 05.13.02 Resveratrol, Spermidine, Fisetin and Quercetin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Quercetin
entries.verdict_text: Ranked 3rd of 4 longevity compounds; little proof for aging
entries.why: Safe in most people at normal doses, but there is little proof for aging, little proof it acts as a senolytic at supplement doses, and most people feel nothing from it.
entries.interactions: Can change how some drugs (e.g. blood thinners) are cleared; check with a pharmacist. Skip with pregnancy, breastfeeding or cancer.
entries.source: 05.13.02 Resveratrol, Spermidine, Fisetin and Quercetin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Dasatinib + quercetin (D+Q)
entries.why: Dasatinib is a cancer-class prescription drug with real side effects. A small study hit the senescent-cell target with no health outcome shown, and an osteoporosis trial found no clear group effect.
entries.source: 05.13.02 Resveratrol, Spermidine, Fisetin and Quercetin

entries.name: Urolithin A
entries.why: Small trials (several involving the maker) improved mitochondrial markers and some muscle-endurance tests in older adults, but muscle size did not change and there is no lifespan proof. The strongest reason: over ~60 and losing endurance, or unable to train hard. Creatine has far stronger proof.
entries.dose_text: About 500-1,000 mg a day; no proof that a higher dose does more.
entries.forms: A product labelled 'urolithin A' with mg stated, third-party sealed; no proprietary blend or 'reverses aging' claims. Pomegranate or ellagic acid products are not the same.
entries.timing: No proven best time; same time each day, with or without food.
entries.cycling: A 12-16 week test; if nothing changed, stop.
test_first: function tests (reps to near failure, timed walk, stairs)
entries.interactions: Skip in pregnancy, breastfeeding, kids and teens. No big interactions known (research is young).
entries.side_effects: Mild, similar to placebo; some mild upset stomach. Long-term safety unknown.
entries.source: 05.13.03 Urolithin A; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Pomegranate extract / ellagic acid (as urolithin A substitute)
entries.verdict_text: Not the same thing as urolithin A
entries.why: They only supply the raw ellagitannins, and the outcome depends on your gut bacteria; many people make little or no urolithin A.
entries.source: 05.13.03 Urolithin A

entries.name: NAC (N-acetylcysteine)
entries.verdict_text: 'Probably gains a trained person without a medical reason little'
entries.why: NAC is a real drug with a few real uses: chronic cough with thick mucus (COPD), some mental-health uses (mixed to modest), and promising small trials in diabetic nerve pain and fertility. As a daily 'just in case' pill for a healthy person the proof is weak, and hard trainers may lose a little training progress. 'Detox', 'immune boost' and 'liver cleanse' claims go much further than the data. Acetaminophen overdose needs the ER, not a store bottle.
entries.dose_text: Usual 600-1,800 mg a day (often split); mental-health trials 1,200-2,400 mg a day. Start low.
entries.forms: Labelled 'N-acetylcysteine' with mg per capsule, third-party sealed; avoid big 'antioxidant complex' products. A sulfur smell is normal (a very strong smell can mean old product). The US FDA legal status is unsettled, so use makers that test each batch.
entries.timing: With or without food; many split into two doses.
entries.interactions: Adds to nitroglycerin's BP drop. At high doses it may thin the blood a little, so check blood thinners or planned surgery with a pharmacist. It does not make alcohol or medicines safe.
entries.side_effects: Upset stomach, nausea, loose stools; rare allergic-type reactions (rash, wheezing).
entries.source: 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: GlyNAC (glycine + NAC)
entries.why: In older adults (a trial of ~24 people over 16 weeks), gait speed rose ~19% along with glutathione, strength and insulin resistance, but the trials are tiny and from one group. Gains may not show in a healthy 35-year-old. Worth watching, not a standard part of a longevity plan.
entries.dose_text: No proven best dose. Practical approach: NAC 600-1,800 mg a day + glycine 3-5 g a day (not the trial dose, which was set by body weight). Start with half the dose for a week.
entries.forms: Basic NAC + basic glycine; skip fancy combination products.
entries.cycling: Set goals first (walking speed, reps, sleep); retest after 12-16 weeks; stop if no change.
entries.interactions: NAC + nitroglycerin adds to the BP drop; mild blood thinning at high doses.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset; large glycine amounts can cause sleepiness.
entries.source: 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Glutathione (plain oral)
entries.why: Oral glutathione is a weak buy with inconsistent studies. NAC and glycine are more reliable. It is overhyped as an antioxidant cure-all, and its 'immune and detox' claims run ahead of the proof.
entries.dose_text: 250-1,000 mg (as sold).
entries.side_effects: Well tolerated; data limited.
entries.source: 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Glutathione (liposomal / sublingual / S-acetyl)
entries.verdict_text: 'May raise levels somewhat. Proof is limited.'
entries.why: These forms may raise levels somewhat, but proof is limited and products vary; be skeptical of untested claims.
entries.dose_text: About 250-1,000 mg a day.
entries.forms: Third-party tested; skip proprietary blends and tiny-amount 'glutathione booster' products (marketing).
entries.source: 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione

entries.name: Glutathione IV drips / injections (wellness, skin whitening)
entries.why: The best evidence is in hospitals (e.g. IV before cisplatin). 'Wellness' shots for energy or skin have no large trial behind them, and regulators have warned against skin-whitening shots. Do not swap hospital cancer treatment for a clinic shot.
entries.interactions: Be careful with asthma or sulfite sensitivity (some products contain sulfites).
entries.side_effects: Injection-site soreness, fainting, rare allergic reactions with fast heartbeat; contaminated batches cause fever, chills and low blood pressure.
entries.source: 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione

entries.name: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA / R-ALA)
entries.verdict_text: 'Best evidence of the three' (diabetic nerve pain)
entries.why: Real but moderate help for burning or tingling feet from diabetes; it does not replace blood-sugar control. Its blood-sugar and weight effects are a small extra at best. No good evidence it slows aging or 'detoxes'; it will not help without nerve symptoms and with normal blood sugar.
entries.dose_text: 600 mg a day.
entries.forms: Plain racemic ALA is fine and behind most research; stabilized R-ALA is stronger per mg and a reasonable upgrade. Seal (NSF, USP, Informed Sport); avoid 'antioxidant complex' blends.
entries.timing: On an empty stomach about 30 minutes before a meal (take with a small snack if it upsets your stomach).
test_first: vitamin B12 (rule out other causes of tingling)
entries.interactions: With insulin or any glucose-lowering pill, low blood sugar is a risk: check with a pharmacist and watch numbers closely in the first weeks. Skip in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
entries.side_effects: Hypoglycemia (shaky hands, sweating, hunger, pounding heart, confusion); rare insulin autoimmune syndrome; stomach upset, skin rash. Repeated lows or rash with facial swelling: get help fast.
entries.source: 05.13.05 Alpha-Lipoic Acid, PQQ and Astaxanthin; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: PQQ (pyrroloquinoline quinone)
entries.why: The story is stronger than the proof: PQQ is still a hope. There is no proof of longer life, muscle or felt energy, and many trials are tiny, short, maker-funded or combined with CoQ10. The same money does more as creatine, protein, vitamin D or a blood test.
entries.dose_text: Usually 10-20 mg a day with food.
entries.cycling: If you try it, judge one thing (sleep or afternoon energy) at 8 weeks and stop if there is no change.
entries.interactions: Skip in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
entries.side_effects: Short-term safe; long-term not studied well.
entries.source: 05.13.05 Alpha-Lipoic Acid, PQQ and Astaxanthin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Astaxanthin
entries.verdict_text: 'A few small human studies, mostly about skin'
entries.why: A safe, optional extra for skin: modest gains in moisture and elasticity after 8-12 weeks. Mixed for exercise soreness; small for tired eyes. No trial shows it protects against disease or extends life.
entries.dose_text: Studies usually used 4-12 mg a day.
entries.forms: Algae-derived softgels with oil, dose in mg (not just 'algae extract'), NSF or USP seal.
entries.timing: With a meal that has some fat.
entries.cycling: Give it 8-12 weeks before judging.
entries.interactions: Check prescription BP or blood-thinning medicine with a pharmacist. Not enough pregnancy or breastfeeding data.
entries.side_effects: Well tolerated; very high carotenoid intake can tint skin slightly orange.
entries.source: 05.13.05 Alpha-Lipoic Acid, PQQ and Astaxanthin; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Antioxidant blends / 'antioxidant complex'
entries.why: You pay for a long label and get too little of each ingredient to matter. Single high-dose antioxidant vitamins have mostly disappointed in big trials and some caused harm; high-dose C and E blunted training gains. 'More antioxidant' is not 'healthier'.
entries.source: 05.13.05 Alpha-Lipoic Acid, PQQ and Astaxanthin; 05.13.04 NAC and Glutathione; 05.06.07 Wastes of Money; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Alpha-GPC
entries.verdict_text: Little in healthy adults; linked to higher stroke risk in one study
entries.why: Not a proven focus pill for healthy people; small gains only in memory loss and stroke recovery, and exercise-power results are small and inconsistent. If you already eat enough choline, an extra capsule probably adds little. High-dose choline pills can raise TMAO, and a large 10-year Korean study linked alpha-GPC use to higher stroke risk (cause unproven).
entries.dose_text: 300-600 mg a day.
entries.forms: Check the actual mg: it is often sold as '50 percent' powder. Food first: eggs, liver, beef, chicken, fish, soy (choline AI ~550 mg men, 425 mg women).
entries.timing: Avoid late in the day (sleep).
entries.interactions: Skip with heart disease or high heart risk at large doses, or on a memory medicine (pharmacist). Don't stack choline supplements or megadose.
entries.side_effects: Headache, dizziness, stomach upset, trouble sleeping if taken late, fishy body smell at high doses.
entries.source: 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Citicoline (CDP-choline)
entries.why: Same verdict as alpha-GPC: not a proven focus pill for healthy people, and a TMAO caution with high-dose choline pills.
entries.dose_text: 250-500 mg a day (check mg of actual citicoline).
entries.timing: Avoid late in the day.
entries.side_effects: Headache, dizziness, stomach upset, trouble sleeping if late, fishy smell at high doses.
entries.source: 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Lion's mane (Hericium erinaceus)
entries.why: It looks safe but is not proven to boost memory or focus in healthy people; small Japanese trial gains faded after stopping.
entries.dose_text: 500-3,000 mg a day of dried mushroom powder or extract.
entries.forms: Fruiting body. 'Mycelium on grain' can be mostly grain starch. Look for stated beta-glucans and an NSF/USP seal. It can also be cooked as food.
entries.cycling: At least 8-16 weeks; as an experiment, take it daily for 12 weeks, watch one thing, stop if no change.
entries.interactions: Skip with a mushroom allergy; no good pregnancy or breastfeeding data.
entries.side_effects: Generally well tolerated; mild stomach upset or skin rash.
entries.source: 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Bacopa monnieri (brahmi)
entries.why: A slow, small-effect herb that is reasonable to try for memory if you are patient: small gains in remembering new information; attention and mood are mixed.
entries.dose_text: About 300 mg a day of a standardized extract (check bacoside content).
entries.timing: With food (an empty stomach often upsets the stomach).
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks; quitting after two weeks is not a fair test.
entries.interactions: May add to medicines acting on acetylcholine and some sedatives; check with a pharmacist.
entries.side_effects: Stomach cramps, nausea, loose stools, dry mouth.
entries.source: 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Ginkgo biloba (leaf extract)
entries.why: For most people ginkgo is an easy skip. A large trial found it did not prevent dementia, healthy people mostly saw no gain, and benefit in existing dementia was small and inconsistent. Raw ginkgo seeds are toxic and can cause seizures.
entries.dose_text: 120-240 mg a day (standardized leaf extract, e.g. EGb 761).
entries.interactions: Raises bleeding risk with warfarin, aspirin and similar drugs, fish oil and other blood-thinning supplements. People usually stop it a couple of weeks before surgery.
entries.side_effects: Headache, stomach upset.
entries.source: 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.06.06 Safety; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: L-tyrosine
entries.why: A tool for a hard day, not a daily habit. It may protect thinking under short-term stress (cold, sleep loss, heavy mental load); in rested, calm people it does very little.
entries.dose_text: 500-2,000 mg (some studies used larger single body-weight-based doses).
entries.timing: 30-60 minutes before the stressful task, away from big protein meals.
entries.interactions: Skip with an MAO inhibitor, thyroid medicine or overactive thyroid; check any prescription.
entries.side_effects: Headache, nausea or jitters.
entries.source: 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Proprietary nootropic blends
entries.why: They often turn out to be caffeine plus small amounts of unproven extras, sold at a high price. If the label hides how much, put it back.
entries.source: 05.13.06 Brain Supplements - Lion's Mane, Alpha-GPC, Citicoline, Bacopa and Ginkgo; 05.06.02 The Short List

entries.name: Curcumin (enhanced absorption)
entries.why: The best-supported anti-inflammatory for joint pain: in knee OA its benefit is close to low-dose ibuprofen and gentler on the stomach. It is not a cure and does not rebuild cartilage. Exercise-recovery effects are small, and there is no good evidence for pain-free healthy people.
entries.dose_text: 500-1,000 mg a day of an enhanced product (phytosome trials ~1 g a day of complex ≈ ~200 mg curcuminoids; piperine ~5-20 mg).
entries.forms: Enhanced absorption: with piperine, phytosome (Meriva), or micellar/nano/liposomal (check the curcuminoids delivered). Label should give curcuminoids per serving, a named tested delivery system and an NSF/USP seal; tampered turmeric has carried lead and dyes.
entries.timing: With a meal that has some fat. Avoid heavy doses right around key workouts (may blunt adaptation).
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks; rate pain 0-10 every 2 weeks and keep it after 12 weeks only if the score dropped noticeably. Stop before surgery.
entries.interactions: Slows platelets, adding to warfarin, blood thinners, aspirin, fish oil, ginger, ginkgo and chondroitin; check with a pharmacist. Piperine blocks liver drug enzymes and raises other drug levels. Binds iron in the gut. Avoid with gallstones or bile-duct problems, liver disease, upcoming surgery, pregnancy or breastfeeding.
entries.side_effects: Upset stomach, nausea, loose stools at higher doses. Rare liver injury, mostly with high-absorption and piperine products: yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, itching or upper-right belly pain means stop and get seen fast.
entries.source: 05.13.07 Curcumin, Boswellia and Other Anti-Inflammatories; 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Turmeric (plain powder supplements)
entries.why: Plain turmeric supplements absorb poorly, so a '1,000 mg turmeric' label tells you very little. Cooking with turmeric is a fine habit but not equivalent.
entries.source: 05.13.07 Curcumin, Boswellia and Other Anti-Inflammatories; 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Boswellia serrata (Indian frankincense)
entries.why: Fewer and smaller trials than curcumin, many maker-funded.
entries.dose_text: Concentrated extracts ~100-250 mg a day; standard extracts up to ~1,000 mg a day, split.
entries.forms: Label should name the boswellic acid content (often AKBA).
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks, one new thing at a time; stop if the pain score doesn't move.
entries.interactions: May affect liver drug-processing enzymes; check prescriptions.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset, nausea, diarrhea; generally well tolerated.
entries.source: 05.13.07 Curcumin, Boswellia and Other Anti-Inflammatories; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Ginger
entries.verdict_text: 'A minor player, not a main treatment'
entries.why: Low-risk and cheap: small benefits for muscle soreness and OA pain, plus a nausea aid.
entries.dose_text: About 2 g a day as powder or extract.
entries.interactions: Mild blood-thinning effect (check blood thinners); adds to curcumin's platelet effect.
entries.side_effects: Heartburn, reflux, loose stools at higher doses.
entries.source: 05.13.07 Curcumin, Boswellia and Other Anti-Inflammatories; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: L-lysine
entries.why: Thin evidence for what it is sold for; cold-sore evidence is mixed and weak. Enough protein almost certainly covers it.
entries.dose_text: About 1-3 g a day if tried.
entries.interactions: Avoid large doses with kidney disease.
entries.side_effects: High doses cause stomach upset.
entries.source: 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: L-ornithine
entries.why: Small studies on tiredness and stress are not strong enough to rely on; hospital liver use is medical, not a supplement benefit.
entries.side_effects: High doses cause diarrhea and stomach upset.
entries.source: 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Proprietary 'amino' / 'recovery' blends
entries.verdict_text: 'Amino insurance' for no reason is a waste
entries.why: Eating ~0.8 g protein per lb covers the conditionally essential aminos. Blends hide small doses, and pricey 'pharmaceutical-grade' or 'instantized' labels add nothing.
entries.source: 05.13.08 Glycine, Taurine and Other Conditional Amino Acids; 05.09.06 EAAs, BCAAs, HMB and Glutamine

entries.name: Probiotics (general, strain-specific)
entries.verdict_text: Strain- and condition-specific; general immunity, weight or mood 'not backed'
entries.why: The answer is 'for some things, with the right strain'. There is reasonable evidence for specific jobs: antibiotic-associated diarrhea (best), some C. difficile prevention, short infectious diarrhea in children, pouchitis and IBS (real but modest). General immunity, weight loss, mood in healthy people, 'detox' and wide-spectrum wellness blends are not backed. For a healthy gut, food often does more than a capsule.
entries.dose_text: Typical ~1-50 billion CFU a day; use the dose tested for your strain. More is not better, and CFU counts can't be compared across strains.
entries.forms: Full genus, species and strain code; CFU guaranteed through expiry; human trials on that exact strain for your problem; third-party tested. Avoid huge-CFU marketing, 'proprietary blends' without strain codes, long strain lists and pasteurized 'probiotic' foods. Follow storage on the label (cold-chain products should ship cold).
entries.timing: With or just before a meal. For antibiotics: start within ~2 days of the first dose, keep going through the course, a couple of hours away from the antibiotic.
entries.cycling: Judge a gut symptom at ~4 weeks and stop if nothing changed; most strains are 'visitors, not residents', so the effect fades when you stop.
entries.interactions: Skip live probiotics if badly immunocompromised, critically ill, with a central line, or with a very short bowel or damaged gut wall (blood infections reported). Stop if bloating worsens through the day (suspected SIBO); don't buy more products to fix the first one.
entries.side_effects: Mild gas or bloating in the first days usually settles; stop if it doesn't. Blood in stool, black stools, weight loss, anemia or night symptoms need a doctor, not a probiotic.
entries.source: 05.14.01 Probiotics; 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Saccharomyces boulardii
entries.why: Among the strongest probiotic evidence: preventing diarrhea during antibiotics in children and adults.
entries.dose_text: Use the dose tested for the strain (typical probiotic range 1-50 billion CFU a day).
entries.timing: Start within ~2 days of the first antibiotic dose and continue through the course.
entries.interactions: Antibiotics don't kill it, but antifungals do, so don't count on it during antifungals. Same live-probiotic exclusions; a yeast blood infection with S. boulardii has been reported.
entries.source: 05.14.01 Probiotics; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)
entries.verdict_text: Best evidence (with S. boulardii) for antibiotic-associated diarrhea
entries.why: One of the two best-evidenced strains for antibiotic-associated diarrhea in children and adults.
entries.timing: Start within ~2 days of the first antibiotic dose; take it a couple of hours away from the antibiotic.
entries.interactions: Same live-probiotic exclusions as probiotics.
entries.source: 05.14.01 Probiotics; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Bifidobacterium longum 35624 (IBS)
entries.why: This strain (and a few studied multi-strain blends) has IBS data, but studies vary a lot and many shelf products have no IBS data.
entries.cycling: Trial ~4 weeks, judged on the symptom.
entries.source: 05.14.01 Probiotics; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Synbiotics (probiotic + prebiotic)
entries.verdict_text: 'The idea is sound' — still strain- and problem-dependent
entries.why: The pairing does not make a weak product strong.
entries.source: 05.14.01 Probiotics

entries.name: Lactase enzyme
entries.why: Reasonable evidence for a specific job: lactose intolerance. Alternatives are lower-lactose hard cheese and yogurt or lactose-free milk.
entries.dose_text: Larger servings of dairy may need more.
entries.timing: With your first bite of dairy, not after.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Alpha-galactosidase
entries.why: Reasonable evidence for a specific job: gas from legumes.
entries.timing: A pill with the first bite.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Pancreatic enzymes (prescription)
entries.verdict_text: Reasonable evidence — only for confirmed pancreatic insufficiency
entries.why: Prescription because it needs a confirmed problem and proper dosing. Signs: greasy, floating, foul stools and weight loss.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support

entries.name: Broad OTC digestive enzyme blends
entries.why: Little good evidence that they help people with normal digestion. If you try one, treat it as a short test and stop if nothing changes.
entries.side_effects: Blood in the stool, weight loss, persistent greasy floating stools, night pain or anemia need a doctor.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Betaine HCl (with pepsin)
entries.why: A reasonable experiment in the right person (real low stomach acid from aging, autoimmune gastritis, H. pylori or long-term PPI use), not a proven protocol. The claims rest mostly on case reports, and trials of whether people feel better are close to absent.
entries.interactions: Never use it with NSAIDs, an active ulcer, known gastritis or acid-reducing medicine. Do not stop a long-term PPI cold (rebound acid).
entries.side_effects: Stop right away if it causes burning.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Digestive bitters
entries.verdict_text: 'The evidence is weak, but the downside is small'
entries.why: Bitter foods or herbs (arugula, dandelion, gentian) before meals.
entries.timing: Before a meal.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support

entries.name: Bovine colostrum
entries.verdict_text: 'A narrow use for hard training and gut health'
entries.why: Early-stage: small, short, often maker-funded trials suggest it may help gut leakiness from hard exercise or NSAIDs and reduce upper respiratory infections in athletes. Immune and muscle-building claims are thin. Only if you tolerate dairy.
entries.dose_text: Usually 10-20 g a day of powder.
entries.forms: Third-party tested powder or capsule; NSF Certified for Sport for athletes.
entries.cycling: Judge after several weeks.
entries.interactions: Skip with a milk allergy; it contains some lactose.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Zinc carnosine (polaprezinc)
entries.verdict_text: 'Thin or early, reasonable only as a short test'
entries.why: A reasonable idea for people who must use NSAIDs (protecting the stomach and gut lining); also tried for stomach upset and ulcers. It is not a cure for 'leaky gut'.
entries.dose_text: About 75 mg twice a day (each 75 mg holds ~17 mg zinc, so ~34 mg zinc a day).
entries.interactions: Do not stack it on top of a big zinc pill; the adult zinc upper limit is 40 mg a day from all sources.
entries.side_effects: Too much zinc over time can push down copper.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Peppermint oil (enteric-coated)
entries.verdict_text: 'Best evidence' of the three for IBS — 'the one most worth trying'
entries.why: Reasonable evidence for IBS pain and bloating: meta-analyses show it beats placebo. Evidence quality is low, but it is a cheap, low-risk trial.
entries.dose_text: Around 180-200 mg of oil before meals, up to three times a day.
entries.forms: Enteric-coated capsules only; do not use a non-coated version for IBS.
entries.timing: Before meals.
entries.cycling: ~4-week gut trial.
entries.interactions: Skip if you already have bad reflux.
entries.side_effects: Reflux and heartburn are most common; stop if you get them.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 'Leaky gut repair' / 'gut healing' blends
entries.why: 'Leaky gut syndrome' is not a recognized diagnosis, and a zonulin number from a wellness panel is close to meaningless. Better barrier support: fiber and plant variety, cutting NSAIDs and heavy alcohol, and treating celiac or IBD.
entries.source: 05.14.02 Glutamine, Digestive Enzymes, Colostrum and Gut Support

entries.name: Glucosamine sulfate
entries.why: GAIT found no significant pain relief versus placebo, and several large reviews found no slowing of joint-space narrowing. It does not repair cartilage or prevent OA. Some people feel a small benefit; many feel nothing. For knee or hip OA, a trial for a few months with low expectations.
entries.dose_text: 1,500 mg a day of glucosamine sulfate, once or split.
entries.forms: Sulfate ('If you try glucosamine, buy sulfate'), single ingredient. With a shellfish allergy, choose a vegetarian or fermented form.
entries.timing: With food to ease stomach upset.
entries.cycling: At least 8-12 weeks before judging; stop if there is no meaningful change. Try glucosamine and chondroitin one at a time.
entries.interactions: Raised INR reported with warfarin, so check blood thinners with a pharmacist. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Watch glucose with diabetes or prediabetes.
entries.side_effects: Mild stomach upset, gas or heartburn.
entries.source: 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Glucosamine hydrochloride
entries.why: The evidence is weaker than for glucosamine sulfate.
entries.source: 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II

entries.name: Chondroitin sulfate
entries.why: GAIT showed no significant pain relief, and combining it with glucosamine did not clearly beat placebo.
entries.cycling: Judge after 2-3 months (8-12 weeks); stop if pain hasn't dropped noticeably.
entries.interactions: Mild antiplatelet effect: caution with warfarin or blood thinners, tell your doctor or dentist before surgery, and don't combine with high-dose fish oil or curcumin without a pharmacist check. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
entries.side_effects: Mild stomach upset. Products can hold less than the label (shark-cartilage sourcing raises quality questions).
entries.source: 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: MSM (methylsulfonylmethane)
entries.why: The evidence for knee OA pain and stiffness (and sometimes post-exercise soreness) is better than nothing but still early. It is not shown to rebuild cartilage.
entries.dose_text: About 1.5-6 g a day, often split into two doses; start low and build up.
entries.cycling: 8-12 weeks (a 2-3 month test, one supplement at a time).
entries.side_effects: Mild stomach upset, gas, loose stools, mild sulfur smell.
entries.source: 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: UC-II (undenatured type II collagen)
entries.why: Much of the evidence is maker-funded and independent results are mixed; be skeptical of megaclaims on type II collagen. It is not the same as collagen peptides.
entries.dose_text: Around 40 mg a day.
entries.cycling: A 2-3 month test.
entries.interactions: Skip with a chicken or egg allergy; be careful with autoimmune conditions (it acts on the immune system).
entries.side_effects: Generally well tolerated.
entries.source: 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: 'Joint complex' multi-ingredient blends
entries.why: They usually under-dose each ingredient compared with studies; a single ingredient at the studied dose is a cleaner test.
entries.source: 05.14.04 Glucosamine, Chondroitin, MSM and UC-II

entries.name: Elderberry (Sambucus)
entries.why: It may shorten a cold or flu by a day or two, but trials are small, short and often maker-funded, with no good proof it prevents illness. Many gummies hold little real extract and a lot of sugar.
entries.dose_text: No standard dose; follow the label.
entries.cycling: Stop after about a week.
entries.interactions: It may stimulate the immune system: check with a pharmacist if you have an autoimmune condition or take immunosuppressants.
entries.side_effects: Raw or unripe berries, leaves, stems and bark contain toxins that cause vomiting and diarrhea; only cooked or properly processed berries are safe.
entries.source: 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Echinacea
entries.why: Results range from nothing to a small benefit for shortening colds; prevention shows no clear effect. Products vary in species, plant part and extract.
entries.cycling: A short course, not year-round.
entries.interactions: Allergic reactions, especially with ragweed, daisy or marigold allergy. Immune herbs can stir up autoimmune and thyroid conditions.
entries.side_effects: Stomach upset is most common.
entries.source: 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Immune shots, fizzy tablets and immune blends
entries.why: You almost never get a real dose of the useful ones. Basics (sleep, protein, moderate training, stress, handwashing, flu shot) come first.
entries.source: 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Saw palmetto
entries.verdict_text: 'Weak DHT blocker with no proof of regrowth'
entries.why: A weak blocker of 5-alpha-reductase, far weaker than the medicines; the studies do not prove it regrows hair.
entries.dose_text: Often around 320 mg a day (fat-based extract).
entries.cycling: If you try it, give it 6 months with photos; if nothing changes, stop.
entries.interactions: Acts on hormone pathways, so avoid in pregnancy.
entries.side_effects: Usually mild, mostly an upset stomach.
entries.source: 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Hair / skin / nail gummies
entries.verdict_text: 'Mostly biotin, with hidden blend doses and added sugar'
entries.why: A small hope, not a treatment. They are mostly biotin, which can wreck lab tests; other ingredients are under-dosed or hidden; label accuracy is weak; and stacking them can push vitamin A and selenium past limits.
entries.forms: If used, choose a USP Verified or NSF seal.
entries.interactions: Stop biotin-containing products at least 3 days before blood tests. Add up vitamin A and selenium across products.
entries.source: 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Finasteride / dutasteride (prescription)
entries.verdict_text: 'The real tools for pattern loss' — prescription
entries.why: Finasteride blocks type 2 5-alpha-reductase; dutasteride blocks both types and cuts blood DHT by ~90%. They need a prescription.
test_first: PSA (finasteride lowers it; tell the doctor)
entries.interactions: Some are not safe in pregnancy. Side effects are possible.
entries.source: 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others

entries.name: Minoxidil (topical)
entries.verdict_text: A real tool (2% recommended for female pattern loss)
entries.why: A real tool for pattern hair loss; the benefit fades if you stop.
entries.dose_text: 2% minoxidil (female pattern hair loss).
entries.cycling: Judge after 6-12 months of steady use.
entries.source: 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others

entries.name: Spironolactone (prescription, hair)
entries.verdict_text: Used for some women; results vary
entries.why: A prescription option for some women's hair loss. Results vary, and regrowth is lost after stopping.
entries.source: 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others

entries.name: Prescription retinoids (tretinoin)
entries.why: Retinoids have the best proof for fine lines and skin texture, along with daily sunscreen, not smoking and sleep. Prescription.
entries.source: 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others

entries.name: Copper peptides (GHK-Cu)
entries.why: Mentioned only with weak evidence (covered in the Peptides volume).
entries.source: 05.14.06 Skin, Hair and Nails - Biotin, Collagen and Others

entries.name: Sea moss
entries.verdict_text: 'Reliably gives iodine' but varies; skip with thyroid disease
entries.why: An iodine and heavy-metal problem, not a 'superfood'. The '92 minerals' claim is marketing, there are almost no good human trials, iodine varies widely by batch, and lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury have been found ('Lead has no known safe level'). A 150 mcg iodine supplement is safer; if you love the gel, treat it as a food in small amounts.
entries.forms: Home-made gels are rarely tested; if used, only a tested brand with heavy-metal batch results.
entries.interactions: Skip with thyroid disease, goiter or thyroid medicine (nodules and autoimmune thyroid are most at risk; high iodine can raise thyroid antibodies). High iodine without enough selenium adds thyroid stress. Pregnant women should not rely on it for iodine.
entries.source: 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Beef organ capsules (desiccated liver, heart, kidney)
entries.why: A 3,000 mg serving is ~3 g of powder ≈ 10 g fresh liver, about one bite. There are no good trials showing they improve energy, hormones or health, so do not rely on a capsule as a substitute for food. Better: a small serving of real liver every week or two, or a targeted supplement for a tested gap.
entries.forms: Third-party seal; avoid proprietary organ blends.
entries.interactions: Add up preformed vitamin A from all sources (chronic >~3,000 mcg/day harms liver and bones and causes birth defects). Men, post-menopausal women and iron-overload gene carriers don't need extra iron. People with Wilson disease must avoid it (copper). Purines can raise uric acid (gout).
entries.source: 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Mushroom blends / mushroom coffee
entries.verdict_text: Look for 'fruiting body' — 'Do not pay extra for the hype'
entries.why: Probably harmless for most people and unlikely to do much. Immunity evidence is thin; lion's mane and cordyceps show only small, short hints. Mushroom coffee has about half the caffeine of a normal cup.
entries.forms: 'Fruiting body' on the label; avoid mycelium grown on grain (can be mostly leftover grain starch). Many labels show no dose; third-party testing matters (heavy metals).
entries.interactions: Check with a pharmacist on immunosuppressants, blood thinners or BP pills. Mushroom or mold allergy is possible.
entries.source: 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Reishi (Ganoderma)
entries.why: Promoted for sleep, stress and immunity; the trending-mushroom verdict applies: probably harmless and unlikely to do much.
entries.interactions: Can lower blood pressure and slow clotting; check with a pharmacist on blood thinners or BP pills.
entries.side_effects: Rare liver-injury reports.
entries.source: 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Chaga
entries.why: Promoted as an antioxidant; probably harmless for most and unlikely to do much.
entries.side_effects: High in oxalates (kidney stones); rare kidney damage reported with heavy use.

entries.name: Turkey tail (Trametes versicolor)
entries.why: Promoted for immunity and gut health; probably harmless and unlikely to do much, with thin immunity evidence.
entries.interactions: Check with a pharmacist if you take immunosuppressants.
entries.source: 05.14.07 Trending Supplements - Sea Moss, Beef Organs, Mushrooms and Black Seed; 05.14.05 Immune Supplements - Vitamin C, Zinc, Elderberry and More; 05.99.02 Nutrition (supplements) — Cheat sheet

entries.name: Black seed (Nigella sativa)
entries.why: Small, short trials suggest modest drops in blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol. Claims about immunity, hair, weight loss and cancer are not proven in people. Products vary a lot in thymoquinone.
entries.interactions: Lowers blood sugar and BP, so check with a pharmacist on diabetes or BP medicine. Avoid in pregnancy.
entries.side_effects: Rash when applied to the skin.
